#533. Is the AI bubble bursting just as Anthropic goes public?

The sharp sell-off in tech stocks after the US midterms has cast doubt on Anthropic's looming IPO. Yet with hundreds of billions still being invested, some think the AI party is still in full swing.

2026 was meant to be the year Wall Street’s trillion-dollar artificial intelligence (AI) bet started paying off. Instead, it’s turning into a test of nerves.

In the first half of the year, many AI stocks hit record highs as US hyperscalers like Google's Alphabet, Meta and Microsoft recorded bumper earnings.

Two of the largest AI players — Anthropic and OpenAI — announced plans for public listings, following SpaceX's much-hyped IPO in June, which briefly made Elon Musk the world's first trillionaire.

AI models, meanwhile, got noticeably better at difficult tasks in the race to beat human intelligence.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

The second half of 2026, however, has brought a lot more uncertainty. While the stock of Nvidia, a chipmaker, pushed even higher last month, many hyperscalers and chip or memory firms have seen their stock prices gyrate wildly.

Then last week, after the Democrats secured control of the United States Congress in the midterm elections, technology stocks sold off dramatically, with the Magnificent Seven — including Meta, Apple, Amazon and Tesla — losing more than $1 trillion in value in a single trading day.

In a further twist, the AI sector took another hit this week as Nvidia shares plunged nearly 10% over two days. The sell-off followed news that Nvidia's board — alongside the FBI — is investigating CEO Jensen Huang’s ties to a woman suspected by US intelligence of being a Chinese spy.

On Thursday, Huang resigned from the chipmaker when a second alleged affair was revealed, sending Nvidia's shares lower still.

Wall Street is growing increasingly cautious about the sheer size of the AI outlay, amid warnings that future earnings may not justify the huge spending. Growing pressure on US lawmakers to curb the expansion of AI data centers has added to those doubts.

In September, investment bank Goldman Sachs estimated that hyperscalers need around $300 billion in annual AI revenue to break even on their spending, leaving a gap of roughly $230 billion.

"We're not in Kansas anymore," Dennis Dick, chief market strategist at the Canada-based Stock Trader Network, told DW, meaning that times have changed. Now, he said, investors are telling companies: "Show me the money."

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Other analysts think it's too soon to expect the AI bubble to burst, including Kit Rees, investment strategist at London-based wealth manager Quilter, who thinks last week's rout was a "healthy correction."

"We’re still in the very early innings of the AI build-out," Rees told DW. "There’s still a lot of excitement around this technology and investors will want to have a slice of the pie."

In addition to the roughly $800 billion invested in capital expenditures this year, AI hyperscalers plan to spend a further $1.2 trillion in 2027 and $1.4 trillion in 2028, according to Goldman Sachs estimates.

While OpenAI has delayed its public listing until next year, Claude-maker Anthropic still plans its IPO later this month. On Tuesday, the company said it would offer 825 million shares at between $70 and $78 per share.

Dick said Anthropic’s decision to go ahead amid the market sell-off left him scratching his head.

While Anthropic had originally targeted a valuation of over $2 trillion, it now thinks the firm could be worth around $1.2 trillion to $1.3 trillion.

Dick said the valuation depends on whether Anthropic can deliver on a forecast by Goldman Sachs of more than $600 billion in revenue by 2030.

"If you get to a company with $600 billion in revenue, [a] $1.3 trillion [valuation] doesn’t sound that bad," he told DW. "But when you’re talking about a company with currently $52 billion in revenue, it sounds like it’s overvalued."

Other analysts, like Vivek Seth, chief executive officer of Shaires Holdings, are more bullish about the Claude-maker's prospects.

"Anthropic is a once-in-a-generation company," Seth told Bloomberg this week, noting how it has grown rapidly and has strong institutional backing. "Its IPO will establish a market-clearing valuation as conditions stabilize."

With many investors already running for the hills, Rees isn’t convinced the AI bubble will burst in the way skeptics expect. She thinks they should watch for stronger signs that the AI trade is maturing.

This could be "a slowdown in AI-related revenues for companies, or signs of less demand or less appetite for financing companies’ AI plans, be it through debt or through equity offerings," Rees told DW.

There are early signs that investors have less appetite for AI-related debt. Borrowing costs for AI infrastructure firms like CoreWeave and Oracle have soared recently. Even the cost of insuring Nvidia’s debt against default has risen 76% in a month, CNBC reported last week.

"They [Oracle] have been spending, some people say, like drunken sailors," Dick told DW. "They’ve compromised their balance sheet to a point where the stock’s fallen 65% from the highs."

That has not stopped Oracle, along with Meta, Microsoft and Alphabet, from continuing to issue new AI bonds. Since the end of last month, the four AI giants have announced deals worth $67 billion.

Rees said another sign could be any new regulations that make it harder to build out US data centers.

This summer, New York and Texas temporarily paused new data center approvals. Texas Governor-elect Gina Hinojosa, a Democrat who takes office in January, wants new laws to stop data centers’ heavy power and water use from pushing up household bills.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

In his upcoming book "AI Mania: Blather, Bluster, and the Bubble of All Bubbles," economist Gary Smith compares the AI boom with earlier frenzies around railroads, automobiles, television and the internet. He warns of a "frightful crash" when the AI bubble eventually pops.

When the dot-com bubble burst in 2000, the tech-heavy Nasdaq stock market index lost nearly 80% of its value. Yet, previous bubbles have often lasted far longer than expected, making the timing of any crash hard to predict.

Joachim Klement, head of market strategy at UK-based investment bank Panmure Liberum, believes a reckoning could happen as early as next year.

"My core conviction is that the AI bubble will either burst in 2027 or in 2028, so sometime in the next two years,” Klement told Bloomberg last month.

#532. Big-ticket holiday items may be harder to find as shipping costs rise

This holiday season, big-ticket items are expected to be in short supply with diesel prices near records, trucking rates close to a post-pandemic level and carrying costs hitting multidecade highs. All of that is forcing many retailers to rethink their holiday inventory strategy.

"We are going to have some of the lowest inventory levels on some of these big-ticket items we have seen in history," said Deborah Weinswig, CEO of retail analytics firm Coresight Research.

Weinswig said retailers she is working with are holding less inventory of big-screen TVs, grills, large consumer appliances like washers and dryers, and other items that take either big amounts of space or cost a lot of money to hold.

"It's freight getting it from there to here; it's carrying costs; then it's just the trucking to get it into the stores," Weinswig said. "We're talking three different pieces right here and each is up significantly year on year."

The surge pricing for supply chain services is being caused by domestic and international policy.

According to Evercore ISI, the rates for general trucking have increased more than 47% year over year during the week of Nov. 2.

Industry experts say a large factor has been a crackdown by the federal government on non-citizen truck drivers and non-U.S.-based truck drivers operating in the U.S. That has created a capacity crunch that has raised rates and is expected to continue to create upward pressure.

At the same time, fuel surcharges are spiking.

Most transportation providers charge customers an extra fuel surcharge to offset changes in the cost of diesel fuel. That surcharge has spiked 64% year over year, according to Evercore ISI data, as diesel prices have hit new record highs due in part to the U.S.-Israel war with Iran.

And inventory holding costs — or the total expense of storing unsold goods, which could include the costs for capital, service, storage and other risk factors — are closely tied to the yield on the 10-year Treasury note, which exceeded 5% in October and remains at multiyear highs in November.

Collectively, the higher costs could mean bigger discounts for shoppers willing to wait, according to Bill Catania, CEO of logistics technology company OneRail, which powers same-day delivery for companies such as FedEx and Lowe's.

"You're going to see more discount and price promotions as we get closer to the holiday to liquidate inventory, so they're not having to transfer it or dispose of it or position it some other way," Catania said.

Retailers are also facing a conundrum in their holiday inventory strategy when it comes to shipping costs versus opportunity costs. In other words, is it worth it to stock up now, or wait it out in hopes that shipping rates will come down some but potentially miss out on having the right product mix?

It's leading to a wait-and-see approach for stocking shelves after early holiday sales in October, executives said.

UPS CEO Carol Tomé said on the company's earnings call on Oct. 27 that it's "just starting to get peak season forecasts from our customers."

Similarly, Derek Leathers, CEO of Werner Enterprises, a trucker for big-box stores and major retailers, said retailers are cautious.

"When rates are higher and the cost of capital is more expensive, you are going to have a much more intense focus on not having excess inventory," Leathers said.

Still, 2026 holiday sales are expected to top $1 trillion as inflation drives growth and customer spending is expected to remain healthy, according to Bain & Company's annual forecast. Leathers said even with the surge in trucking and shipping rates, he's seeing that retailers are willing to pay up to stock up.

"The bigger concern right now is wanting to make sure they have their capacity locked in. There is way more dialogue around the assurance of having a truck or whatever mode that needs to be secured," Leathers said. "Not saying they are price insensitive, because they are certainly always concerned about price. But you can't sell it if it's not on the shelf."

ShipMatrix, a data analytics firm for the logistics industry, forecasts 2.4 billion packages will be delivered during the 2026 holiday peak, a 4% increase year over year.

It's an increase that will likely lead retailers to increasingly use gig delivery, especially later in the holiday peak. Gig workers allow retailers and delivery companies to adjust to changes in order flow and accommodate surges of last-minute shopping without spending time and money onboarding new team members.

"Gig economy delivery is great. You know, it fulfills fast, but there's better unit economics out there," Catania said.

Industry experts said they also expect to see more retailers use drones for last-mile delivery for smaller items.

A 2024 PwC study forecast that the cost of drone delivery would "drop by more than 70% over the next 10 years, which will not only match traditional last-mile delivery costs, but surpass them and create an inflection point for the industry."

Amit Regev, CEO of drone company Flytrex, said the company is in active talks with retailers about using drones for holiday deliveries.

"The expectation now is becoming so much more instant," Regev said.

Retailers have been increasing their use of drones. Lowe's in September said it was launching a drone delivery service in partnership with DoorDash and Alphabet's Wing. Amazon earlier this year said it was aiming to offer drone deliveries in nearly 500 U.S. cities and towns by the end of the year.

Flytrex currently delivers for Walmart and a number of restaurants including Little Caesars and Papa John's.

"Customers are looking for that instant gratification," Regev said. "So if it takes too long, they might not want to order with you. And from what we are seeing that's a stronger incentive for them to try and test or deploy deliveries using drones."

#529. Oobah Butler Can Sell You Anything—If You’re a Rich Idiot

You’d think that Oobah Butler would have run out of schemes by now.

The gonzo British documentarian’s repertoire includes creating an entirely fake restaurant—The Shed at Dulwich—and getting it to the top spot on London’s Tripadvisor; selling bottles of Amazon drivers’ urine on the ecommerce site; and convincing venture capitalists to give him $1 million.

But as his new HBO show, Oobah: Scams for a Better Tomorrow, makes perfectly clear, Butler still has plenty of tricks up his sleeve—and it’s a delight to watch them unfold.

The series launches November 22. Each of the premier season’s five episodes centers on Butler scamming his way into success in a different industry—wellness, wine, dating, music, and a finale I do not want to spoil—with increasingly outlandish ideas that, somehow, almost no one advises him against.

His shock of bleach-blond hair and appearance of a Victorian ghost notwithstanding, there are undeniable similarities between Butler’s style and that of master of manipulation Nathan Fielder. Both use satire and parody to make social commentaries, and both often divert from their original plans by hyperfocusing on what the average person might consider a tangential detail, carrying these side quests to extreme lengths. But while Fielder has sometimes been criticized for roping unassuming working-class folks into his hijinks, in Butler’s case the joke is almost always on the rich and powerful—and the systems that allow them to prevail.

“The whole show can be reduced to ‘monkey see, monkey do,’” Butler tells me from a coffee shop at the New York Historical Society in Manhattan, where he’s just ordered a latte with four espresso shots and been recognized from TikTok by a fellow patron. “I just find these bad actors and copy them.”

Butler’s knack for convincing high-profile—in some cases notorious—executives and tastemakers to appear on camera and earnestly weigh in on his ridiculous plans at times boggles the mind. In the series premiere, he sets out to start a wellness company that sells the tears of human children as a skin serum, and gets none other than former Theranos chief creative officer Patrick O’Neill to consult on a marketing strategy.

Applying his characteristic charm, Butler tells O’Neill he “smashed it” with creating mystique around the scandal-plagued biotech startup, to which O’Neill replies, “Thank you, yeah. I think it’s good to share the knowledge.”

Butler wearing glasses designed to collect the tears of children.

After briefly expressing hesitancy around the ethical sourcing of the tears, O’Neill begins offering Butler packaging advice: a tear-shaped bottle, and the two discuss the name Lacrimé (“tears” in Italian). “It makes it feel exotic and not necessarily something you’d see from Johnson and Johnson,” O’Neill says, in all seriousness.

Confiding in $1,500-an-hour lawyer Jennifer Keller about how he may have committed fraud with his wellness venture, Butler tells her the industry is “a gold rush of bullshit. And I want in.” She laughs and says that he sounds “more and more like an American.” It’s all very funny, but as the name of the show hints, there is a Robin Hood quality to Butler’s scamming, in this case exposing the poorly regulated nature of skin care and supplements.

Butler has chosen the New York Historical Society as our meeting point because he loves history, and New York’s in particular. When he first moved here in February 2024, he started reading Robert Caro’s The Power Broker, a biography of influential urban planner Robert Moses, giving him an understanding of “how power works” in the city. But his itch to move came well before that, when he visited in 2016.

“I just found it so inspiring,” he says, dressed in a maroon velvet shirt, baggy dark jeans, and Salomon sneakers, a Patagonia backpack slung over his shoulders, as we set out for a walk in Central Park. “I got to an age where I just thought, well if I don’t do this now, I probably am not going to do it.”

Although New York is indeed full of power brokers—and very wealthy ones at that—he says it’s different from the aristocracy he grew up around in Feckenham, a 700-person “Hobbiton-style village” in the UK.

“I grew up in a lower-class family … I’ve definitely got a bit of a chip on my shoulder about class,” he says, noting that he’s the youngest of six siblings. “And America, for all of its issues, there is something amazing about how I see the same guys who really wind me up in the UK—upper-class kind of guys—and the way that they walk the earth and the way they feel and the way they carry themselves. I see them come here and no one gives a shit. Really, truly, no one gives a shit.”

Butler didn't go to college. He started a band called My Grey Horse in 2010, playing guitar and singing. Around the age of 17, he began writing music reviews, secretly hoping to score his band some coverage. “It was a scam on the go,” he says. But he caught the writing bug, finding it “meditative.” Later, he joined VICE (where I previously worked as a senior reporter) as a freelance video host, making a bunch of documentaries, including the extremely viral one about The Shed. From there, he did several films for the UK’s Channel 4 and cohosted MTV’s Catfish UK.

“It changed my life and was absolutely the right thing to do. I wouldn't have been able to afford to move here if I hadn't done Catfish,” he says.

Though he tells me he’s not a comedian, Butler is a natural clown, and at times even just his buffoonish mannerisms are enough to elicit laughs. Maybe he’s such a natural because he comes from a long line of schemers. He tells me his great grandfather moved to the US in the late 19th century as part of the fur trade, but he would also sell rabbit droppings rolled in flour as medicine.

“I'm cut from a line of people who sell shit,” he says.

Though he may not have firsthand experiences, Butler’s perceptions of hoity-toity cultural institutions—and their vulnerabilities—are spot on. In an episode about fine wine, he embarks on a mission to sell a smoke-tainted swill brand called Fumare as a high-end product—even though it would normally be tossed by wine producers or used for barbecue sauces. Part of his task is to convince New York Times wine critic Eric Asimov to give the smoked wine a good review.

Butler creates a psychological profile of Asimov, determining that he’s a “contrarian” who “wants to be romanced.” Knowing he’s a fan of Bob Dylan, Butler just happens to be playing a Dylan song on the piano when Asimov shows up for a tasting. While Asimov pans the first glass of smoky wine, Butler tries again, by pretending it's actually a glass of Barolo, the same stuff Asimov says he fell in love with when he first got into wine. “I have no complaints,” Asimov says—an endorsement that Butler promptly attaches to Fumare’s label.

In another episode, Butler starts an AI dating company called Sole, but instead of matching people with a chatbot, as he’s purporting to do, he matches them with other humans to see if they connect.

“The idea was that people trust in the technology more than a conversation with one another,” he says.

These days, many of Butler’s stunts either directly or indirectly relate to Big Tech—for good reason.

“A lot of it is built on speculative promises and the idea of utopia rather than connected to reality. Tech CEOs constantly coming out and lying about what they’ll be able to do in 10 years to shit-coin their stock price,” he says, adding that the sector is “riddled with inauthenticity.”

Despite having the backing of HBO, his own work still feels authentic and haphazard, as opposed to overly polished. He says it’s usually just him and a couple of other people carrying out the stunts. “One of the episodes was basically me and me in my bedroom,” he says, noting that while he’s been working on the finale for six years, originally envisioning it as a feature film, all the others except for the pilot were shot in the last eight months.

“There’s a DIY characteristic to the stuff anyway, and I want the people watching to not feel excluded from the pieces of it. And that's always a thing where I'm like, ‘Oh, if the budget for the show was much bigger, it might not feel like this anymore,’” he tells me.

Considering all the pranks he’s pulled off, I ask him point-blank if it’s a bad idea for people to answer the phone when he calls. He rebuffs, pressing me for my take.

Truthfully, I think there’s a high chance that if you engage with Butler on camera, you’ll come off looking like a fool—particularly if you’re someone with any type of clout. But for the sake of my own entertainment, I hope people keep doing it.

#524. Are Smart Car Seats Worth It? I Tested Two to Find Out (2026)

Car seats had some pretty humble beginnings. Even I, an early-’90s baby, slightly recoil every time I see a picture of myself strapped into a flimsy plastic bucket with a loud geometric-print cover that once held my life in its clutches. Car seat design and safety standards have come a long way, and today’s models are quite souped up, with cup holders, rotating bases, and enough bells and whistles to rival an Escalade. And now, they’re getting smart.

Many car seat manufacturers are adding technology to, for lack of a better term, give parents a second set of eyes. Think Bluetooth-connected chest clips, sensors, apps, and real-time alerts that ping your phone if something goes awry, whether that’s an installation issue or if a chest clip comes unbuckled while the car’s moving.

It sounds appealing, right? Especially for parents who already have plenty to worry about and are often juggling a million things just to get out the door in the morning. But it’s worth asking: Do these features actually make car seats safer? Or are parents paying for peace of mind?

I tested two smart car seats, the Babyark Classic ($799) and the Cybex Cloud G Pro ($550), to see if this technology lives up to the hype and whether a smart seat is worth adding to your registry. Because while an app-connected car seat might seem cool and offer some reassurance, no amount of technology can replace proper installation and use. Keep in mind that they’re not exactly apples-to-apples comparisons; the Babyark is a convertible car seat designed to grow with your little one, while the Cybex is an infant carrier. I tested the Babyark with my toddler daughter and the Cybex with my infant son, giving me a chance to see how each one worked at different stages of parenthood. But both offer a glimpse into how companies are integrating technology into car seats, and I wanted to see how they perform in everyday life.

Many smart car seats revolve around sensors. Some come equipped with sensors that help caregivers determine if the seat is installed correctly. Others use Bluetooth-enabled chest clips to send notifications to your phone if the chest clip breaks free mid-ride or if you walk away from your car while your child is still buckled in. A few models even have crash detection, which can send notifications to designated emergency contacts if a collision is detected.

The biggest difference comes down to how the technology is integrated. Some models, like the Cybex I tested, rely on a Bluetooth chest clip that connects to an app. Babyark takes a slightly different approach, with mechanical indicators on its Classic model and a swankier electronic sensor system built into the base of its higher-end Smart and Premium models.

The first thing I noticed about the Babyark out of the box was its base setup, which was different from any other car seats I’ve used. The base is a spaceship-looking device with a fold-out support leg and anti-rebound bar. The seat itself is pretty bulky, but I didn’t mind too much, since by the time I started using it, my daughter was old enough that I didn’t need to haul her around in an infant seat anymore.

Car seat installation can be an exercise in patience, but I found setup pretty straightforward. The Babyark app walked me through every step, with video tutorials for each stage. Once everything was in place, indicators on the base glowed green. (Red means something’s off.)

The app is easy to navigate, but once I installed the seat, I pretty much forgot about it. I enabled notifications in case something needed attention, but in my several months of using the seat, nothing has warranted an alert so far, aside from the occasional random disconnection.

It’s worth noting that the Babyark offers different versions of the seat, all with different technology. The Classic model, which I have, currently retails at $790 and offers guided installation videos and mechanical indicators. Babyark's Smart and Premium models—which retail for $999 and $1,190, respectively—add features like forgotten child alerts and impact detection. That’s a roughly $200 to $400 jump, which is worth considering if you’re particularly interested in those features.

You can check the app for basic statistics, like how much time your child spends in the seat, but I haven’t felt the need to follow this closely. More importantly, I didn’t find myself opening the app to monitor the seat while my daughter was in it. At the end of the day, the Babyark feels like a regular car seat to me. But a great, sturdy car seat at that!

I also tried out the Cloud G Pro, which comes with SensorSafe, a Bluetooth chest clip that communicates with the Cybex app on your phone. Pairing the clip, which looks and functions like any other, with my phone was easy peasy. When I intentionally tested the alerts, they worked as expected and came through almost immediately.

The temperature notifications worked, but almost too well. SensorSafe sends an alert when your car’s interior climbs to above 95 degrees Fahrenheit or drops below 45. Depending on the weather, your car might already be outside that range when you first get in, and it takes a little time for the cabin to warm up or cool down. So don’t be surprised if you get an alert before the AC or heat has a chance to do its thing.

SensorSafe can also alert you if the clip becomes unbuckled while driving or if you leave your child buckled in the seat and walk away with your phone. In the latter scenario, the default setting has your phone loudly announce “CHILD IN CAR!” in a man’s deep voice, which scared the hoots out of me the first time it went off. If you don’t respond to the alert (you can stop or snooze it), the app will notify your emergency contact and share your location.

Like the Babyark, I didn’t find myself opening the Cybex app very often to check on things. I mostly let it run in the background and waited for notifications rather than actively checking in on the system. The alerts worked just fine, but I used the app so infrequently that my phone eventually offloaded it.

As appealing as all those gadgets and gizmos sound, car seats aren’t foolproof. “These are supplements. They're not substitutes,” says Jennifer Booge, a car seat safety expert with the National Safety Council. “We have to make sure that we're understanding how to use the car seat correctly, because there is so much to know, and every car seat is so different.”

According to data collected through the NSC’s National Digital Car Seat Check Form, a little over 72 percent of car seats entered into the system have some form of misuse. Manufacturers are working to address these issues with installation videos and app-based guidance, but Booge says there’s still not enough research to determine whether smart features actually improve safety.

Some car seat manufacturers offer access to certified child passenger safety technicians who can walk you through installation questions. I experienced this firsthand with the Babyark. Even after following the app’s instructions and getting the green light that everything was secure, I still had some reservations about how much the seat was wiggling. I reached out to the company, and they virtually walked me through the installation. (Which turned out to be correct; car seats are supposed to have a slight wiggle, no more than an inch back and forth.)

“Don't be afraid to pick up the phone and call or schedule that virtual appointment and meet with those experts that are there to help you, because it's not easy,” Booge says. “Every car seat is different. Every vehicle and car seat combination is different.”

As Booge points out, tech can be useful even when it isn’t built into the seat itself. The rise of virtual appointments gives caregivers access to certified technicians that they may not otherwise have available. At the end of the day, a car seat doesn’t need a battery or an app to do its job, and all the technology in the world can’t replace knowing how to use it properly.

Do you need a smart car seat? Probably not. After testing the Babyark and the Cybex Cloud G Pro with SensorSafe, I’m not totally convinced the added tech is worth paying a premium for. Both offered features I appreciated, and they certainly gave me peace of mind, but neither fundamentally changed how I use a car seat day to day. I’d rather prioritize a seat that fits my child and my vehicle, and that I can use correctly, rather than pay extra for an app I rarely open. All in all, my biggest takeaway is not to mistake more features for more safety.

#519. Germany gives sweeping powers to police, intelligence services

Drone sightings and cyberattacks have heightened security concerns. How are the police preparing to meet these challenges? And how do intelligence services plan to counter threats from both domestic and foreign sources?

Germany's intelligence agencies have been given wide-ranging new powers. The lawmakers in the Bundestag agreed to a reform package on Friday.

Under the new rules, the Federal Intelligence Service (BND), Germany's foreign intelligence service, will be allowed to respond to cyberattacks by foreign powers with counterattacks of its own. The range of possible measures is broad, from deleting and manipulating data to disabling entire systems and, if necessary, even destroying physical weapons such as drones that could be deployed against Germany.

Under certain conditions, the agencies will also be permitted to enter homes and business premises covertly, for example, to prepare surveillance operations. They will, however, not be allowed to use force against people. An independent oversight board is to be established to monitor the agencies.

Opposition lawmakers specializing in domestic policy warned against granting powers that are too broad.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

The president of Germany's Federal Criminal Police Office (BKA), Holger Münch this week again pointed out that today's hybrid attacks pose a new challenge to the organizations safeguarding the country's security. At his organization's annual meeting in Berlin this week, he said the "hybrid attacks" are challenging the "separation principle," which means that the police conduct investigations while intelligence services gather information. The exchange of data between the two is permitted only under strict conditions.

Münch has long objected to this strict division of responsibilities. He has been calling for expanded powers for the police and closer cooperation with the domestic intelligence agency, the Office for the Protection of the Constitution, which is responsible for countering espionage and sabotage.

The separation principle results from lessons learned from the Nazi dictatorship, when the Secret State Police (Gestapo) operated largely outside judicial constraints and served as the regime's central instrument of terror, used to oppress and murder Jews, Sinti and Roma, homosexuals, communists, social democrats and many others. The Allied powers that defeated Nazi Germany in World War II then decided that the police and intelligence services should remain institutionally separate and be granted different powers.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Historian Sönke Neitzel of the University of Potsdam considers the separation principle understandable in its historical context. At the BKA's autumn conference, however, he described it as "nonsense" in light of today's threat landscape and said it was no longer necessary in a country that has been a constitutional democracy for decades.

While Neitzel considers the separation principle outdated, German Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt of the center-right Christian Social Union (CSU) wants to preserve it in its essential form. In his view, even a more extensive exchange of data does not violate the principle. At the same time, however, he has made clear that he wants to transform the domestically focused Office for the Protection of the Constitution and the BND into "real intelligence services."

This legislative reform brings Dobrindt a significant step closer to that goal. Parliament approved the interior minister's plans with the votes of the governing coalition of the conservative Christian Democratic Union and Christian Social Union (CDU/CSU) and the Social Democratic Party (SPD).

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Dobrindt insisted that Germany intends to take an active approach to defending itself against cyberattacks: "Anyone who attacks us in this way must know that we are prepared to strike back. They must know that their digital infrastructure, their server infrastructure, and their software will also be targeted by us."

BKA President Holger Münch welcomes Dobrindt's determination and points to the growing threat posed by cyberattacks. The line between criminal and state-sponsored actors is becoming increasingly blurred, he argues. As a result, both intelligence services and law enforcement agencies face the same challenge.

To underscore the scale of the threat as he sees it, Münch cited two statistics: in the first six months of 2026, crime originating from abroad rose by 24% compared with the same period the previous year. What concerns him most is that fewer than 5% of these cases are solved. The BKA chief considers this trend more dangerous than ever: "The state's promise of security can become fragile. Confidence in the ability of its institutions to act effectively and remain steadfast is declining."

This article was originally written in German.

#517. Tesla’s Cybercab Is the Subscription Hell They Told You Not to Worry About

There is always a catch. Or in the case of Tesla’s self-driving Cybercab, several.

Last Friday night, Tesla said it had invited “select customers” to purchase their very own Cybercabs. The two-seat, gold vehicle is unlike any other on the market: It lacks a steering wheel and brake pedals, and is primarily driven by software. (Other autonomous vehicle companies, including Alphabet's Waymo and Amazon’s Zoox, offer self-driving rides on ride-hail networks, but don’t let people buy their cars.) Tesla’s "limited release” will supposedly offer some people (unclear how many) the opportunity to pay $29,900 to take delivery in December.

From there, though, the Cybercab will need constant cash infusions to stay on the road.

The business model raises questions about what people will actually get when they buy a Cybercab. “You’ll never really own the car,” says Ivan Drury, the director of insights at Edmunds. “It’s more like $30,000 to buy into a franchise.”

According to documents posted on Tesla’s website, the vehicle “will not operate” without what Tesla is calling an “autonomy subscription," a monthly fee that will start at $299. If owners don’t pay on time and in full, their self-driving cars won’t work. If they try to operate the vehicles in areas that don’t support the service—right now, they’re restricted to portions of cities in Florida and Texas—their self-driving cars won’t work. (That area can expand, contract, or “relocate” at any time.)

If owners do anything that Tesla deems "unauthorized or inappropriate," the company says it can suspend or cancel the subscription—and their self-driving cars won’t work. If the vehicle loses connectivity, the self-driving cars won’t work. (“Tesla is not responsible for carrier, spectrum, environmental, or other external outages,” its “autonomy agreement” says.)

Tesla also reserves the right to make an owner’s car not work at any time: It says it can, for any safety or security purpose, suspend or terminate access to Cybercab tech, or restrict operations by location, road type, weather, or “condition.” This is particularly salient because the Cybercab is also under investigation by US safety regulators, who are trying to understand why Tesla believes the vehicle meets safety standards without so many of the parts and systems required.

Tesla didn’t respond to a request for comment.

For years, automakers have seen increasingly software-dominated vehicles as an opportunity to get drivers hooked on the same special sauce that makes Netflix, Amazon, and Spotify so potent: monthly subscription services. Because these vehicles can receive over-the-air software updates, manufacturers can offer drivers new services as they make them. The upside is high, tech-style margins that keep rolling in, versus the razor-thin ones seen in car-making. A 2024 report suggested that connected-car features could one day be a $200 billion industry.

In some ways, the subscription model is working. Today, some automakers charge extra for remote start, security, internet connectivity, and advanced driver assistance features. General Motors said it made $2.7 billion in subscription-related revenue last year from fees drivers paid for its OnStar and Super Cruise services.

But some customers have also found the business model yucky, or even offensive. Why charge extra to “unlock” a feature that’s already built into a car? If an automaker can add a new feature at any time, can’t they also take it away? And if they can take it away, what does "ownership" mean? In 2022, BMW told drivers in select countries it would activate factory-installed heated seats for a monthly or one-time fee; it eventually backed down after public outcry, pledging the company would no longer charge subscription fees for pre-installed hardware. (BMW is still pursuing a subscription model for some features.) “Consumers hate being nickel-and-dimed for subscriptions,” says Drury.

Tesla was an early mover in the subscription feature space and has offered connectivity and driver-assistance features for monthly or one-time fees for a decade. As the company has shifted away from making cars and toward robotics and autonomous vehicles, executives have made clear that charging for services is the future. (Its Robotaxi service currently picks up fare-paying passengers in parts of eight US cities.) So Tesla buyers may be particularly amenable to paying monthly to make their self-driving cars go.

In exchange for monthly fees, buyers will also get access to other services, too, including remote support, roadside assistance, tire, air filter, and windshield wiper replacements, and tire and camera inspections. (The agreement says that list might change, too.) Cybercabs will be able to “travel autonomously, unoccupied to a Tesla service center,” the company says. The fee doesn't cover insurance.

Cybercab buyers will have other restrictions. The vehicle is for personal use only. Even though CEO Elon Musk has repeatedly said owners will be able to put their vehicles on Tesla’s wider Robotaxi network to make money during downtime, and even has an online interest form for those who want to own and operate their own Cybercab fleets, the current ownership agreement prohibits that. Buyers are also prohibited from selling or transferring their vehicles without Tesla’s written consent. The company “advises against” children under 13 riding in the Cybercab, and prohibits children from riding without an adult present.

In a post on X, Musk showed no apparent compunction about the Cybercab business model, but did say the monthly price for autonomy “is too high.” He wrote that the price should be “more like ~$115/month.”

#512. AI Told These Ex-Google Guys How to Build a Billion-Dollar Weapons Business

When Silicon Valley entrepreneur Chad Steelberg decided he wanted to get involved in the war in Ukraine, he had no idea where to start. So the then CEO of enterprise AI company Veritone did what he knew best: built an artificial intelligence model to help him figure it out. Today, he has proprietary munition and missile designs, several government partnerships, and a defense-as-a-service business valued at more than $1 billion.

Steelberg, alongside fellow Google alumnus and former Apple executive Andy Baynes, says they are trying to break the Russia-Ukraine war “stalemate,” Silicon Valley–style. They believe their experience building and iterating technology quickly can help bring Western weapon manufacturing in line with the rapid innovation cycles seen on the battlefield and beat the “attritional cat-and-mouse technology game” that the war, as Baynes describes it, has become.

Steelberg, originally from Newport Beach, California, started itching to “make a difference” on the battlefield after he took in a couple hundred Ukrainian refugees into his French chateau in early 2022. He says he was regularly “heartbroken” by the outpouring of grief whenever bad news arrived about a husband, father, or son back home. “I believe I could really change the outcome of this and every war,” Steelberg tells WIRED. "I'm not saying this is purely altruistic,” he adds. “Of course we're going to be making money doing it."

This week, their firm, Tiberius Aerospace, said it had secured $85 million in Series A financing, led by European technology investment firm Lakestar and Rochefort Asset Management, a national-security-focused investment firm licensed under the US Defense Department. Ukrainian venture capital firm UA1 is also an investor.

Tiberius began as Steelberg’s private research lab, incorporated in 2021, which employed people across France, the UK, and US to experiment on left-field ideas across a range of technologies, from drones and electric vertical takeoff aircraft to quantum computing. After the invasion, he pivoted the lab’s AI and aerospace engineers into writing code and building spreadsheets to objectively analyze the war’s many factors and calculate what could move the needle. The AI model they created quickly ruled out building better defensive technology because that would just harden the stalemate.

With his aim narrowed to building an offensive weapon, Steelberg developed several metrics to numerically analyze the lethality of different systems, including cost-effectiveness, and used the AI engine to simulate weapons under different conditions and identify what would disrupt the market. Don’t build another drone, it suggested, build longer-range artillery munitions. The resulting system, called Sceptre, can be fired from a 155-millimeter howitzer—the most common artillery weapon donated to Ukraine. As well as traveling farther than currently available rounds, they claim they can reach supersonic speeds and altitudes beyond jamming range.

Giving Ukraine’s guns extra range is important, Sam Cranny-Evans, an associate fellow at UK defense think tank the Royal United Services Institute, tells WIRED, because it would allow Ukrainian gunners to operate beyond the reach of Russian drone attacks. 155-mm shells “can cause massive damage to a group of vehicles or infantry,” he says. “Any technology that can help Ukraine extend the reach of its howitzers and return them to combat would be valuable.”

With a prototype he’d designed with the help of AI, Steelberg also started to expand the Tiberius team, including bringing on board Baynes as chief strategy officer in 2023. Baynes had first traveled to Ukraine around a decade ago to investigate how local startup Ring, now owned by Amazon, had outdone Nest, which he’d been working on and eventually sold to Google. He fell in love with Kyiv’s ambitious software engineers and booming tech scene–responsible for globally successful tech tools like Grammarly and Snapchat’s face filters. In 2016, he bought a local life-science tech company with the aim of accelerating next-generation medicines through automating clinical trials and improving protein modeling. “What drew me into Kyiv was the hunger and ambition in the engineering community,” he tells WIRED. “It was difficult to not be enormously attracted to that and to see if it's something that could be put into really critical-mission problem sets like cancer drugs or speeding up clinical trials for life-science companies.”

After the Russian invasion, Baynes set himself up in Budapest for around six months to help with the logistics of evacuating women and children and moving equipment into the country. He asked his global network for help finding medical equipment, vehicles, and accommodation for refugees—bringing him back in touch with Steelberg. Baynes believes the West’s response to the invasion has been “inadequate” and that Ukraine needs better offensive capabilities to push Russia’s army back.

In April, Tiberius announced it had successfully fired one of its Sceptre projectiles from a NATO-standard 155-mm howitzer for the first time. It is now working with the US Army to mature the system, and it has announced a $500 million technology collaboration contract with UK partners to manufacture, license, and distribute the munition. It is also developing a missile, which it expects to start generating revenue next year.

Tiberius has turned the AI system it initially built into a product called GRAIL (Generative Real-Time Artificial Intelligence for Lethality). Steelberg says he is “most excited about” this. He hopes the platform can enable continuous upgrades to the weapon designs Tiberius licenses by decentralizing manufacturing. Steelberg says that, as well as automating supply chain management and compliance, the software simulates weapons against different targets in a range of environments and weather conditions, such as an Arctic peninsula. In addition to open-sourced data, the team is trying to get hold of much sought-after active combat data from around the world, including Ukraine. The idea is that this all enables users to test, iterate, and design weapons for specific uses much quicker.

“In the world of AI and design and development getting faster and faster, what is it that the West or the group of allied nations have an undeniable advantage on?” Baynes asks. “If you can weaponize all of the spare capacity and precision manufacturing across the UK, France, Germany, the Nordic countries, the US,” he says, “that's something that our adversaries today can never ever match.” Tiberius aims to achieve this by copying “the Apple model,” continues Baynes, who reported to Steve Jobs for four years. He says outsourcing manufacturing to many third-party subcontractors can accelerate development and deployment and keeps expensive production costs off Tiberius’ balance sheet during peacetime.

“We're taking the approach of Silicon Valley,” says Steelberg. “When you run into a big, hard, hairy problem, you not only cross that, but you turn around, you build a bridge—it’s a toll bridge, obviously—so the entire industry can cross that hurdle faster, better, stronger. They might pay a small fee, but it's better than dying in the ditch and not making it across it.”

#511. Novo says Wegovy injection lowers BMI and obesity rates in children in trial

Novo on Monday released full results from a late-stage trial showing its blockbuster Wegovy injection helped children ages 6 to under 12 with obesity shed weight, significantly lowering their body mass index.

Wegovy reduced BMI by an estimated 19.7 percentage points on average compared with a placebo at 68 weeks, with BMI falling 17.4% among children receiving the drug and rising 2.2% among those receiving a placebo. Those results assumed patients stayed on treatment during the trial.

When evaluating all children in the study, including those who discontinued treatment, Wegovy lowered BMI by an estimated average of 16.2 percentage points more than the placebo at 68 weeks. All 167 kids in the study received lifestyle modifications throughout the trial, including a ​reduced-calorie diet and increased physical activity.

The detailed results mark an encouraging step forward in treating childhood obesity — a chronic disease that can carry serious cardiovascular, metabolic and psychosocial consequences but has had few treatment options for younger children. When left unaddressed, childhood obesity can extend into adulthood, bringing earlier and more severe health complications.

"This is a very significant disease burden in this very young patient population," said Dr. Andrea Traina, Novo's medical director lead of obesity.

In 2025, the disease affected an estimated roughly 177 million children and teens ages 5 to 19 worldwide, according to the World Obesity Federation. That figure is projected to rise to 228 million by 2040.

While Wegovy is already approved to treat obesity in children ages 12 and older, there are currently no approved medications for those under 12. The latest results offer evidence that Wegovy can potentially fill that treatment gap, safely and effectively reducing the severity of the disease in children as young as 6.

In Novo's trial, 85% of children started with moderate to severe obesity, which corresponds to BMI thresholds of 35 and above and 40 or higher, respectively. Nearly half already had at least one obesity-related complication, such as high blood pressure, high cholesterol or sleep apnea.

But more than 40% of children treated with Wegovy were no longer classified as having obesity after 68 weeks of the trial, assuming patients stayed on treatment. Novo initially shared that result in September.

"We are driving towards control of this chronic disease in that patient population when they are still so young and at such high risk for more advanced and accelerated disease progression because they developed it so early," Traina said.

Novo said Wegovy's overall safety and tolerability among children — how well patients managed the drug — were consistent with those seen in ​trials ⁠with adults. The company added that it observed no safety concerns related to growth or pubertal development in the kids.

Still, the two-year study does not establish whether treating obesity earlier can change its long-term trajectory, or what treatment and maintenance might look like as children grow into adulthood, Traina said.

"That is something that is still an evidence gap," she said, pointing to the potential of future research.

#510. The tiny camera tech creator Austin Evans uses for almost everything

After 17 years of making tech videos online, Austin Evans has used his fair share of complicated camera gear. These days, he'd rather keep things simple.

When Mashable asked Evans what creator essentials he keeps close at VidCon 2026, the longtime YouTuber started with the obvious answer for someone who's made a career obsessing over gadgets: not one phone, but two. Then there's the tiny camera that has become one of his most versatile pieces of gear — a far cry from the enormous, expensive cameras his team once relied on.

Here's what Austin Evans keeps in his bag.

"The phone's got to be number one," Evans said. Although in his case, "phone" is technically plural.

Evans uses an iPhone primarily for shooting video, and the convenience means he can respond almost immediately when a story breaks.

"There was so much news," he said of that day's tech cycle. "I was walking into the parking garage, and I'm shooting Shorts on my phone and just sending them off to my editor."

For everything that isn't primarily video, Evans also carries a Samsung Galaxy Z Fold. His reasoning is straightforward: He likes having the bigger display inside.

Together, the two devices let him shoot, work, and keep up with an industry where news can break while he's literally walking through a parking garage.

Then there's the piece of creator gear Evans really wanted to talk about: DJI's tiny Pocket cameras. "Those cameras have been so fantastic, especially if you're on your own," he said.

They're small, stabilized, can track a subject, and can easily move between vertical and horizontal shooting — all qualities Evans thinks make them particularly useful for solo creators. His own Pocket camera has certainly been put through its paces.

"The amount of times we've had that thing strapped with a suction cup to the front of a car driving on a racetrack," he said.

When it's not speeding around a track, he has another job for it. "I plug it into my desk. It's my webcam." Evans paused. "I feel like it's a giant ad. It's not."

More than any individual gadget, Evans' creator essential is really a philosophy: The easier the tech makes it to start filming, the better.

His team once used a RED camera that he remembers as "absurdly expensive and hot and heavy" — exactly the sort of equipment designed with a full film crew in mind.

Today's smaller cameras may not replace every piece of professional equipment, but that's not really the point. "You can get legitimately really good stuff that is not crazy expensive and, most importantly, feels very much designed for a solo creator," Evans said.

"Just pull it out of your bag, press three buttons, pair a mic, and you've got fantastic-looking results."

After 17 years of creator tech, sometimes progress looks like carrying less of it.

#508. How a Bunch of YouTube Auteurs Are Reinventing Hollywood

The mad scramble to score Imax tickets for The Odyssey was about as intense as the Trojan War, and the Marvel Cinematic Universe showed signs of resurgence with Spider-Man: Brand New Day’s $2.5 billion global haul. But the biggest buzz of the 2026 summer movie season? Two small-scale horror films from a couple of young YouTube auteurs.

First came Obsession, from 27-year-old Curry Barker, which made more than $500 million worldwide on a budget of less than $1 million. The film follows a meek young man named Bear, who yearns to be in a romantic relationship with his friend Nikki and uses a magical object to make his wish come true. By turns moody, funny, and shocking, Obsession proved that audiences are hungry to talk about something other than reheated IP. Barker got his start with the YouTube sketch comedy channel That’s a Bad Idea, while 21-year-old Kane Parsons gained a cult following on the platform by experimenting with visual effects and creepy atmospherics. A series of short films Parsons made in his teens culminated with the release of Backrooms in May. The feature picked up the narrative from those earlier YouTube videos, which were themselves inspired by an old 4chan meme and internet folklore around the idea of haunted liminal spaces.

Parsons’ avid fandom anticipated a big-screen Backrooms long before he signed with A24, making the movie a guaranteed hit. Backrooms earned $400 million worldwide on a budget of $10 million, surpassing Marty Supreme as the studio’s highest-grossing movie ever. The film stars Chiwetel Ejiofor as Clark, a depressed divorcé who runs a failing furniture warehouse and vents about his ruined marriage to his therapist. One night, when investigating his store’s glitchy electrical system, he stumbles through a wall and into an apparently infinite maze of fluorescent-lit hallways that contain what seem to be deconstructed or misremembered pieces of the real world—and perhaps some living entities as well.

Though Backrooms stands alone as a hallucinatory vision of a vast, ever-expanding unreality just outside our own, many critics also read it as commentary on the state of generative artificial intelligence, which mindlessly reproduces and regurgitates its training data in permutations that often don’t make sense. Whether Parsons intended that interpretation or not, he spoke out against AI several times following the movie’s release, calling it “a symptom of a broader cultural and economic rot.”

The people, inventions, and viral moments that made 2026 a little more bearable.

Something we missed? Let us know in the comments.

Then there’s Zach Cregger. While not a YouTuber per se, he got his start in sketch comedy (The Whitest Kids U’ Know) and this year followed 2025’s Weapons with a 2026 adaptation of Resident Evil.

Parsons told WIRED earlier in the year that he imagines his cohort of directors will bring certain YouTube sensibilities to Hollywood. “I don’t think there’s a lot of Instagram filmmakers or a lot of TikTok filmmakers that go for long-form content in a way that would actually be looked at or respected as film,” he says. “So it feels like YouTube is the only viable avenue in that way, in an actual meaningful mainstream context.” Among the crop of twentysomething filmmakers entering the industry today, “I think it’s very unlikely that you would have a filmmaker who is sort of reaching that place right now and getting that kind of media attention who has not at some point in the last 20 years put stuff on YouTube,” Parsons says.

Studios have certainly taken notice, scouting the site’s horror content for fresh talent and aggressively pursuing breakout projects. After a screening of Barker’s Obsession at the Toronto International Film Festival in 2025, A24 and Neon embarked on a bidding war for the film before it was picked up by Focus Features for roughly $15 million.

Netflix reportedly also lost out on a bid to take Obsession straight to streaming; it’s possible that other young directors will follow Barker’s example in pushing for theatrical release.

The YouTube generation is proving that the internet can supply whatever education you might need on your path to the red carpet. While Hollywood consolidation threatens to stifle creativity, a new wave of artists are betting on themselves—and some are winning.

#506. 'We slept here': Flight delays linger as airlines recover from ground stop, but schedule improves Monday

U.S. flights delays eased on Monday as airlines scrambled to get back on track after the Federal Aviation Administration grounded departures nationwide for more than four hours on Friday.

Nearly 300 U.S. flights were canceled and close to 1,000 were delayed Monday, a fraction of Sunday's disruptions, according to FlightAware data.

Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy over the weekend tied the issue that prompted officials to call for the ground stop to a router in southern Arkansas and work to update copper wires to a fiber-optic system overseen by L3Harris Technologies. FAA Administrator Bryan Bedford said the upgrades were part of "routine" maintenance to switch over to fiber optic.

Officials ordered the ground stop before 4 p.m. ET on Friday and it lasted until after 8 p.m. ET, marking the longest halt to U.S. flight departures since 9/11.

Hundreds of thousands of travelers were stranded and about 18,000 U.S. flights were canceled from Friday through Monday morning, according to FlightAware.

Over that period, American Airlines had the most cancellations with 5,367 flights, close to 22% of its schedule, followed by Delta Air Lines with 3,434 cancellations, or 17% of its schedule, according to aviation data firm Cirium. Southwest Airlines and United Airlines each canceled more than 16% of their schedules. Bad weather on Thursday and Friday had also contributed to disruptions before the ground stop.

On Sunday, disruptions lingered but were starting to improve.

"We slept here," said Beth Martin, who was trying to travel home to Birmingham, Alabama, from New York's LaGuardia Airport on Sunday at the end of her daughter's birthday trip. The two were booked for Saturday night, and when delay announcements started rolling in from Delta, they decided to make good use of the extra time: After strolling through Central Park, they went window shopping on Fifth Avenue.

But when the flight was canceled, the standby list for a backup flight looked grim and their original midtown hotel was charging about $700 for an additional night, the two slept at LaGuardia on Saturday. She said they found wheelchairs to sleep in outside security.

Airlines waived change fees and fare differences and offered pilots and flight attendants extra pay to ease the delays.

Customers told CNBC they were booked on several flights before getting on board.

Justine Fritz, who works in sales for a consumer goods company, was in New York for a business event on Friday. She tried five different flights before getting on one to Houston, then flew four hours out of her way to get back to Minneapolis after her Saturday flight was canceled. Fritz said she had so many boarding passes that the Transportation Security Administration wouldn't let her through security at first.

"It's been bananas," she told CNBC at the gate. Fritz said she made the best of it by shopping and getting a haircut, but she's still disappointed.

"I'm missing the first hour of the Vikings game," she said.

Martin said her trip home with her daughter will take even longer. Delta booked them to Memphis, and her husband will drive the four hours from Birmingham to pick them up.

Officials are investigating the root cause that led to what the FAA described as "instability" in data feeds. Duffy said Sunday that two routers, the original one detected as a problem in southern Arkansas, and another in Amarillo, Texas, are in an L3Harris lab in Florida.

"We are supporting the FAA in its investigation to understand the conditions that led to the Nov. 13 ground stop of our nation's air travel," L3Harris said in a statement Saturday afternoon.

President Donald Trump said Monday he didn't "take any responsibility" for the ground stop.

Shortly after the ground stop, Duffy said he was asking Congress for as much as $50 billion for upgrades to the aging U.S. air traffic control system. A day later, Democratic lawmakers pushed back, citing unspent money from existing funding, which includes Congress' approval last year of $12.5 billion for airport and air traffic control improvements over five years.

"Our committee, on behalf of the flying public, will hold the administration accountable for what happened to make sure this chaos does not happen again," said Reps. Rick Larsen, D.-Wash., ranking member of the House Committee on Transportation and Infrastructure, and Andre Carson, D.-Ind., ranking member of the aviation subcommittee, in a joint statement.

#505. Oura launches Jet Lag Plan, letting users hack their travel

Oura Ring users who are always on the go are about to benefit from a feature to combat jet lag. Jet Lag Plan is a new Oura feature that creates a plan to navigate time changes before, during, and after travel.

We have all been there with travel. As much fun as the vacation is, if you're dealing with time zone changes, jet lag can totally kill the vibe. You don't want to waste a moment in a new place by taking a nap back at the hotel. Oura wants to help its Oura Ring users combat jet lag with its latest feature. The new feature is built off of a National University of Singapore study that used 1.5 million nights of sleep data from de-identified Oura users. The best tech deal this week The Apple iPhone 18 Pro is free right now with T-Mobile

The Apple iPhone 18 Pro is free right now with T-Mobile

Jet Lag Plan builds a plan designed just for you. It uses your flight itinerary along with your sleep patterns and chronotype to craft a series of recommendations. It produces a personalized schedule around sleep, light exposure, activity, and caffeine for journeys that cross three or more time zones.

The feature uses Oura's AI-powered support, Oura Advisor, to adjust the plan as travel changes, in case things don't go as expected. Jet Lag Plan will be available globally to users with Gen 3 or newer hardware on both iOS and Android, as long as users have their language set to English.

So if you're traveling for the holidays, don't let jet lag stop you from your vacation or family time.

#504. Ice hockey impasse as Russia threatens sanctions on Canada, Germany

Two weeks after the CAS ordered ice hockey's governing body to reintegrate Russia into international play, a solution remains elusive. Now Russia has threatened to take legal action against two tournament hosts.

"Should Canada and Germany refuse to allow the Russian team to participate, we will demand compensation, enforce the postponement of the competitions, and impose sanctions on the organizers," Russian Ice Hockey Federation President Vladislav Tretiak told the TASS news agency.

"There are rules: if a team does not take the ice, it receives a forfeit loss and sanctions are imposed," Tretiak said after a presidential sports council meeting in Moscow on Thursday.

"The IIHF as a way out — either allow us to participate or, if we cannot enter Canada, move the championship, don't hold it at all, or impose sanctions on Canada."

The threat comes after the Canadian government confirmed Wednesday that it would not allow Russian players to take part in the IIHF World Junior Championship starting on December 26 in Alberta.

"Canada's position is unequivocal: as long as Russia continues ⁠its war of aggression ​against Ukraine, there can be no return to business as usual," Adam van Koeverden, Canada's secretary of sport, said in a statement on Wednesday. "Canada will continue to stand with Ukraine."

Following the Court of Arbitration for Sport (CAS) ruling in late October, in which it said the security concerns the IIHF cited for barring Russian teams from taking part in international tournaments was not sufficient, the world governing body pledged to work to comply with the decision.

On November 8, Norway said it had been bumped from the World Juniors tournament and had been informed by the IIHF that Russia would take its place. Several other national hockey associations said they had received a revised schedule for the tournament and stated they would not play against Russia. The IIHF has not confirmed the change.

Germany has been watching developments related to the World Juniors and host nation Canada closely, as it is set to host the IIHF World Championship in Gelsenkirchen, Mannheim and Düsseldorf starting on May 14.

With several nations saying they will not play Russia and major sponsors threatening to pull out, a German government spokesman described the prospect of hosting the tournament under these conditions as "effectively impossible."

However, Germany has ruled out taking the Canadian approach.

Ronald Rauhe, Germany's minister of state for sport, said Wednesday that refusing to grant visas was "not a solution for the [German] ice hockey federation [DEB], nor is it a solution for successfully hosting a world championship anywhere."

At the same time, though, he expressed support for the DEB in its wish to host the tournament as planned.

"We believe that we should channel all our energy and efforts into helping sport — and ice hockey in particular — find a solution, which would, of course, entail excluding Russia from the World Championship."

What makes things even more complicated for German officials are concerns that taking a hard-line on Russia could jeopardize Munich's chances as it bids to host the Summer Olympics in 2036, 2040 or 2044.

The International Olympic Committee (IOC) recently lifted its sanctions on Russian athletes and suspension of the Russian National Olympic Committee, opening the door for their return to competition despite the ongoing war in Ukraine.

The thinking goes that the IOC would expect national Olympic committees bidding to host an Olympic Games to follow its lead. The IOC is set to decide in the next few weeks whether Munich advances to the next stage of the process.

For now, though, the ball appears to be in the IIHF's court, after Ottawa confirmed its refusal to grant Russians visas to play in the World Juniors. How the dispute regarding that tournament gets resolved could go a long way to finding a solution for the men's tournament in Germany in May.
