#468. Xreal Aura Review: Stunning Screens, Frustrating Controls

Smart glasses company Xreal has released its magnum opus—the Xreal Aura, a $1,279 pair of extended-reality glasses that runs on Google’s Android XR platform. The Aura glasses can project virtual screens into the wearer’s field of vision and include augmented-reality elements for use in the real world.

The Aura glasses arrive just before the first wave of Android XR glasses from Google and Samsung, in partnership with glasses manufacturers Warby Parker and Gentle Monster. Those devices aim squarely at Meta’s smart-glasses empire. But the Aura glasses are more like virtual reality headsets, now in a more comfortable, glasses-like design. They go head-to-head with Meta’s VR Glasses, slated for release in early 2027.

The first big caveat about the Aura glasses is that they’re wired. A long cord hooks onto the end of one of the glasses’ arms via a USB-C cable. That cord connects to an attached compute puck, about the size of a smartphone and weighing a little more than a half-pound. It comes in 12 or 16 GB storage options and has a battery that powers the glasses for roughly four to five hours with constant use.

When the Aura glasses work, they’re wonderful. The glasses are pretty lightweight, at 95 grams. A four-mic array sits in the arms with Bose EQ tuning that sounds great. (You can also connect wireless headphones.) The display screen has a 1920 x 1200-pixel-per-eye resolution that is noticeably better than other Xreal glasses I’ve worn. A 70-degree field of view means the screens and virtual elements pop up in a wide frame of the wearer’s vision. That means the outer edges of your view will still be the real-life room around you. That can help if you’re trying not to fall over, but it can also be noticeable when trying to feel immersed in a movie.

The big thing about Aura is that you can, in theory, run every app that already exists on Android. Xreal has a few primary categories for how it expects people to use its Aura glasses. The big one is entertainment. Like other Xreal glasses, the Aura can project a screen right in your field of vision. You can watch movies, TV shows, or YouTube videos, right in your field of view. The virtual screen stays fixed, or it can follow you around as you turn your head. You can also unplug the glasses from the compute puck and use them as display glasses to extend your Steam Deck’s screen, for example, though I had issues with that when playing more graphics-intensive games like Cyberpunk 2077.

The Aura glasses attach to a compute puck for processing, which also doubles as a battery.

The other big use case is productivity. The Aura glasses can host virtual workstations that let you swap between tabs and keep multiple tasks running. So you can have a Google Doc right in front of you, Spotify to the side, and those Slack messages you keep ignoring in the back. If you’ve ever wished you had even more space to stash all your browser tabs, this is the device for you. Pair it with a Bluetooth keyboard, and you’ll have a whole workstation on your face, even on a plane, without having to crane your neck awkwardly at a laptop. I wrote almost half this review with the glasses as my screen, but eventually swapped back to a regular desktop to give my eyes a rest.

There are also augmented reality experiences, like using Google Earth to turn a room into a 3D model of a city that you can stomp around in like Godzilla, plus immersive virtual tours so you can see exotic places like the Galapagos.

Two lenses are set in the frame, one smaller lens behind the other. The smaller lens carries the display and AR elements, popping them up within a 70-degree field of view. The outer lens can go from perfectly see-through to very dark. Turning up the darkness makes it easier to see the projected virtual screens. Turning the darkness down enables a much clearer pass-through, which can help you avoid tripping over things while walking around.

That said, these glasses aren’t really meant to be worn while walking around. Even with no AR elements enabled, the double-lens layout feels distracting. There is also no way around the fact that these glasses are still pretty chunky. If you can rock the thicc fit, then great, but I’ve gotten some pointed stares when I walk around with them.

The compute puck can be used as a trackpad to navigate the interface, and it also has a fingerprint sensor.

The glasses do feel lightweight, but after a few minutes of use, they start to heat up. When I take them off, they leave red divots on the bridge of my nose. It’s a small price to pay, though, and it doesn’t ruin the experience. Compare that to something like a VR headset, which does offer better immersion but at the cost of being heavy and uncomfortable to wear for long stretches.

The compute puck can be an annoyance. It’s light enough, but using the Aura glasses means you have to carry yet another thing that is strapped to the device on your face. There were some smart choices made on the puck, like a fingerprint sensor for biometric authentication, and the puck’s surface works like a trackpad to move the onscreen cursor. That seems much smoother than reaching out to control the device with hand movements, but the trackpad wasn't very precise either. Which is a shame, as it would be ideal for someone on an airplane, say, who wants to control the device without punching the seat in front of them.

Controls are the biggest problem I’ve had with the Aura. The front cameras track your hand movements. Hold out your hand and pinch two fingers together to open up an app or move a window. It works most of the time, but some gestures don’t always register. I find myself trying to open Spotify or switch between titles on Prime Video and have to repeatedly pinch the air in front of me for anything to happen. When people have been around to see me, they’ve told me I look like I’ve gone bonkers, just grunting and wildly pinching thin air.

The Xreal Aura glasses are a stunning display of how far smart-glasses technology has come. But they still feel like a novelty that most people won’t want or need. They haven’t quite solved the core issues facing the product category—looking like a dork or being effortlessly comfortable to wear. But they do feel like a big step in the right direction. If only they could get a pinch more usable.

#466. Gen Z protests: Do Baby Boomers really have it better than young people?

Should young people in Germany be more worried about their future than Baby Boomers were in the 1980s and 1990s? Or should both generations take to the streets and protest together? DW checked the data.

Young people across Germany and Europe are taking to the streets, voicing fears of a bleak future.

But is that really the case? Does Gen Z face greater challenges than Baby Boomers did in the 1990s? What do the two generations have in common, and where do their experiences differ?

"Of course, it's fair to ask, 'Were things just as tough for you back then?'" youth researcher Simon Schnetzer tells DW. "But young people see that things are difficult for them now, and say that's why they need support today."

Schnetzer, who wrote the annual Youth in Germany study, highlights one key question raised by the recent demonstrations across Europe as: "Have we given young people the conditions they need to live and work here with confidence, and to keep this system funded?"

His straightforward answer is no. A survey of the statistics shows that both Gen Z and the Baby Boomers are affected by major societal changes, but in different ways. DW surveyed data on pensions, education, housing and climate change to find out more.

The facts point to a clear trend: Fewer and fewer young people are having to support an ever-growing number of retirees. According to the Germany's public pension insurance system, there were 3.73 contributors for every retiree in 1957. By 2025, that figure had fallen to just 2.1.

By 2045, this number is projected to drop to just 1.73 contributors per retiree. In absolute terms, this means 35.35 million contributors will be financing pensions for 16.82 million retirees.

To cushion this trend and keep contribution rates stable, the pension system already receives around €118 billion [$131 billion] in annual government subsidies. This amounts to roughly 25% of the federal budget. That means an increasing share of the population will be called upon to help fund pensions.

There are also signs that many people's pensions are already falling short of covering their living expenses. The number of retirees relying on federal basic income support has risen from 257,000 in 2003 to 738,000 in 2024.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Rising rents hit low-income households particularly hard. According to a report by the German Institute for Economic Research (DIW), the share of income spent on rent by low-income households rose from around 24% in 1990 to nearly 36% in 2021.

This means that in 2021, the lowest-income households spent an average of 14 percentage points more of their income on rent than high-income households.

According to Germany's Federal Statistical Office (Destatis), in 2025, an average of 11% of the population spent more than 40% of their disposable income on housing costs. Among people at risk of poverty, the figure was as high as 35%.

However, according to calculations by real estate platform Jacasa, Boomers could actually help ease pressure on the housing market in the coming years. They currently own around 4.8 million owner-occupied houses and apartments.

Over the coming decades, these properties are expected to change hands as former occupants sell them, move into assisted living, or hand them down through inheritance. In some regions, this could lead to an oversupply of properties and, consequently, lower prices, according to Jacasa's projections.

According to the federal government's Education Finance Report, public spending on education for people under 30 has doubled since 2011, rising from around €4,000 to approximately €8,000 per person annually.

Despite this increase, Germany ranks only in the middle of the pack internationally. According to the Federal Statistical Office (Destatis), public education spending accounted for 4.6% of Germany's gross domestic product (GDP) in 2022, compared with an OECD average of 4.7%.

However, the additional funding cannot solve the problem of teacher shortages. According to estimates by the Standing Conference of the Ministers of Education and Cultural Affairs, Germany will be short of around 27,000 teachers by 2035. The main reasons are the wave of Baby Boomer retirements and declining birth rates, which have contributed to a shortage of young teachers.

Back in 1972, the Club of Rome warned of the consequences of global warming in its landmark publication The Limits to Growth. According to the United Nations, the planet is on track for 2.6°C of warming by the end of the century compared with pre-industrial levels.

If the world maintains its current climate policies, children who are six years old today could experience heat waves two to seven times as often as Boomers did over their lifetimes. That was the finding of a 2025 study by Vrije University in Brussels.

The deadly impact of extreme weather is already evident in rising death tolls during recent heatwaves. According to Germany's Robert Koch Institute (RKI), an estimated 16,000 people died from heat-related causes across Germany by mid-September 2026. The vast majority — more than 14,000 — were over the age of 65.

"Gen Z and Baby Boomers are in the same boat. We need to bring them together, because otherwise younger people have no prospects for prosperity, and neither do older generations," youth researcher Schnetzer concludes.

He suggests that both generations take to the streets and protest together, adding that would just be the beginning. "What needs to follow is a constructive process to define goals and measures that everyone can support," he said. "Even if it means making sacrifices."

#464. VSCO Is Gunning for Adobe Lightroom With Its New Desktop App

New photographers looking for inspiration often start with an app like VSCO. The popular mobile app, launched more than a decade ago, is known for one-click presets that emulate film and make it easy to elevate a photograph before posting it to social media. But as newbie shutterbugs level up their craft, they often graduate to an app like Adobe Lightroom and its more professional tool set.

VSCO's pitch is simple: Keep photographers in the ecosystem by building a desktop app to rival Lightroom. On Tuesday, the company announced that its Studio Pro Desktop app is officially landing on macOS, following the launch of Studio Pro on iOS earlier this year. Neither version is available on Android or Windows, though the San Francisco–based company plans to port the apps in the future.

“We're helping shape these folks in their formative years,” VSCO CEO Eric Wittman tells WIRED. “We've got to keep giving them more bricks to build upon their own personal, creative journey—not just their creative journey, but also help them build a career.”

The desktop client is one part of VSCO's growing portfolio that caters to full-time photographers. Subscribing to VSCO One, for example, nets you access to Studio Pro, additional presets, and VSCO Workspace—a customer relationship management tool for handling contracts, booking, and scheduling. It also includes VSCO Galleries to send finished work directly to clients and VSCO Sites, a portfolio website builder to find new clients. All of these apps and services launched in the past year.

Access to the broad suite costs $500 a year, or you can get the Studio Pro mobile and desktop apps alone with a VSCO Pro membership for $5 per month ($60 annually). There is also a free tier, but some tools are locked behind the subscription. (Naturally, the original VSCO app is still around for enthusiasts.)

The Studio Pro Desktop app is speedy, features more than 200 presets, and supports RAW editing for 20 camera brands. Batch editing is the highlight, letting photographers edit up to 500 images simultaneously to speed up workflows while preserving the original files. Previews are rendered in real time, and at the end, users can export the final images directly to VSCO Galleries (or wherever they'd like).

I've been trying the app for a few weeks, and it is snappy. It loads RAW files quickly, and it even supports keyboard shortcuts. The sheer breadth of presets is also really nice, even if I tend to tweak colors myself. But there's a catch. If you're like me and coming from Lightroom, you'll miss a few features that Studio Pro Desktop doesn't offer yet. For example, Masking, Curves, and the Erase function (aka the spot removal tool) are “coming soon.”

“We want to be simple, intentionally, but we want to be powerful with our tools,” says Kyle Hale, VSCO's senior product manager. He says the app will feature around 70 percent of what people need for desktop editing, with the rest coming through regular software updates. While he doesn't expect full parity with a competitor like Lightroom by the first quarter of 2027, Studio Pro Desktop will have “the meat of what those programs offer.”

Companies like Adobe have heavily leaned into generative AI in their creative editing tools. While VSCO uses AI and machine-learning models in some tools like the upcoming Erase and retouch tools, the company says it doesn't train its own models on anything that people post on the VSCO app. VSCO also relies on some third-party models, like those from Black Forest Labs, but it has agreements in place that third parties cannot train on its user data.

“I don't think all AI is bad,” Wittman says. “But to be very, very clear: Generative AI, or if you're replacing the photographer—like what you're seeing with what Meta is doing, what Adobe's doing, like almost every other company is doing—we are not doing that. We stand by and champion photographers first and foremost, and that's not going to change.”

#463. Should I buy a gaming console just to play GTA 6? That depends on your FOMO.

Grand Theft Auto VI is out extremely soon, if you hadn't heard. Are you prepared?

By that, we mean do you have a PlayStation 5 or Xbox Series console at the ready for Thursday's big launch? If not, you're going to miss out on the biggest gaming launch of this year and many other years. FOMO is a natural human reaction to these sorts of things, and here at Mashable, we fully understand the pain of not being sure whether or not you should buy a console just for GTA 6.

So, let's lay out the cases for and against doing that.

The primary and most obvious reason to buy a console for GTA 6 is that it's the only real way to play it at launch on Nov. 19. There is technically another way that we'll cover in a little while, but for all intents and purposes, you cannot have the same experience everyone else is having without buying a PS5 or Xbox Series console.

We don't know this yet for sure, but there's a possibility that GTA 6 is an incredible video game. You probably wouldn't want to miss out on that. What are you going to do while everyone else is having an amazing time parading through Leonida, read books? Come on, that sounds boring.

One thing that's also worth remembering is that other video games exist. A lot of them, in fact. If you buy a PS5 or Xbox Series console, you'll have access to the last six years of current-gen releases, some of which are extremely good. They might even be better than GTA 6! As a fun bonus, through the magic of backward compatibility, ports, remasters, and remakes, you'll also be able to play countless video games from previous generations of hardware, too.

Lastly, both consoles (at least the models with disc drives) work as 4K Blu-ray players, if you're into collecting physical versions of movies. That's cool, too.

Both consoles have been hard to find in stock (thanks in large part to GTA 6), but the Xbox Series S and PS5 Digital Edition are both in stock at Amazon, as of this writing.

First, foremost, in the biggest, boldest font you can imagine: You shouldn't buy a console just for GTA 6 because they're stupid expensive these days.

Both Xbox and PlayStation have recently increased the prices of their consoles due to real-world economic concerns. The cheapest model right now is a $499 Xbox Series S, and Rockstar hasn't shown us that version of the game yet, leading to speculation that the game is better on PS5, which starts at $599. If you want the best possible version at launch, you'll need a PS5 Pro, which costs $899 — and is currently out of stock at most retailers.

In other words, there just isn't a particularly affordable way to play GTA 6 traditionally at launch, unless you already own the hardware.

There are, of course, other reasons to not get a console for GTA 6. There exists a slim likelihood that the game just isn't that good, though again, we have no idea at the time of publication. It also won't have an online component at launch, and no one knows when it will get one. For a lot of people, GTA Online is the only GTA experience that matters, and that audience will have very little to do in the new game until some nebulous point in the future when Rockstar decides to cater to them.

Maybe you just don't care that much about non-GTA video games, either. If that's the case, it's hard to recommend spending this much money on a box that will only play one game.

There are two main ways to play GTA 6 without buying a PS5 or Xbox Series machine. One of them doesn't sound all that great, while the other one will require some patience.

To be clear, there are multiple massive reasons why you might not want to do this. For starters, it involves a monthly subscription. Beyond that, Microsoft recently imposed strict monthly hour limits on Cloud Gaming. With this system, you will be able to play at most 15 hours of GTA 6 per month. Many people are going to play more than that in the first weekend it's out. Even if those aren't concerns, game streaming is subject to the limits of your home internet, meaning that latency and buffering can and will occur. That version of the game will also be visually downgraded to some degree, per Rockstar.

If game streaming (understandably) doesn't work for you, the last option is to wait for the PC version. Unfortunately, Rockstar has not said anything about when GTA 6 will launch on PC, though a recent report pegged it as coming in early 2027. That will likely be the best version of the game in terms of visuals, but only if you have the requisite hardware. For those who already have capable gaming PCs, this might be the best option for playing GTA 6, provided you're patient enough to wait. For those who don't, this is going to be even more expensive than buying a console, so maybe don't bother.

#461. Turkey uses espionage accusations to pressure government critics

The arrest of a German foundation's employee in Istanbul this week has put the focus back on pressure tactics used by the Erdogan administration. The arrest is far from the first of its kind.

When police officers appeared at her home in Istanbul last Wednesday evening, Yonca Verdioglu Sik was surprised — even more so when they took her in for questioning. Her lawyer says she was accused of political and military espionage.

But, according to transcripts of the interrogation that were published later, Verdioglu Sik was never asked any questions about espionage. Instead the public prosecutor's office appeared to be more interested in the activities of her German employer, the Heinrich Böll Foundation.

For 18 years, Verdioglu Sik, who was born and raised in Germany, has been the foundation's project coordinator. In her role, she organizes projects that focus on democracy and the rights of women, minorities and LGBTQ+ people.

During the interrogation, transfers of money from the foundation into her bank account were discussed. Verdioglu Sik found out that she was now also subject to a travel ban.

Verdioglu Sik was eventually released, but her arrest caused outrage among critics of the Turkish government. She is married to investigative journalist and member of parliament, Ahmet Sik. He belongs to the left-wing Workers' Party of Turkey, or TIP, and is known as one of the harshest critics of the current government.

Sik has recently been looking into a stock market scandal, which allegedly benefited members of the ruling Justice and Development Party, or AKP, headed by Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan, and associates.

Opposition critics drew a clear conclusion: As a member of parliament, Sik has parliamentary immunity. So instead, the justice system is putting pressure on him through his wife.

"If you take away a state's law, what is left is no longer called a state, but a gang," Sik responded to the arrest in writing.

Verdioglu Sik's arrest is not the first such case in Turkey. Ever since the attempted coup against the Erdogan government in 2016, accusations of espionage have been leveled at a wide variety of groups in Turkey: journalists, opposition figures and human rights activists as well as employees of foreign embassies and staff of foreign institutions like nongovernmental organizations and foundations.

Such accusations have often been followed by acquittals or convictions for other offenses, albeit sometimes years later. But what the many instances have in common is what's known as a "chilling effect." Any investigation can mean lengthy pre-trial detention, reputational and professional damage and even social isolation.

In the past, such cases have even triggered diplomatic spats.

In 2015, for example, Can Dundar and Erdem Gul, both senior journalists at the opposition daily Cumhuriyet, were accused of espionage after reporting that Turkey had tried to ship arms to rebels fighting the Syrian government. Dundar now lives in exile in Berlin.

In 2017, Erdogan said that reporter Deniz Yücel, then working for German newspaper Die Welt, was a "German agent." That led to a serious diplomatic crisis between Berlin and Ankara.

Espionage charges have also been laid against local employees of the US diplomatic corps and against a lawyer working for the German embassy. US pastor Andrew Brunson and his wife were also arrested because of alleged links to Kurdish anti-government groups. Turkish philanthropist and human rights activist Osman Kavala, who was charged with espionage and attempting to overthrow the constitutional order, remains in prison.

Most recently, espionage charges have been brought against the former Istanbul mayor and Erdogan's political competitor, Ekrem Imamoglu, and a number of journalists.

Hakki Tas, a research fellow and expert on Turkey at the German Institute for Global and Area Studies, said the number of such cases have been increasing over the past few years.

On the one hand, Turkey has the right to protect itself from foreign intelligence services — especially given geopolitical competition and conflict in the region, he argued. On the other hand, there's a long tradition of bringing the Turkish opposition to court to face security charges.

"What foreigners or employees of foreign institutions have experienced in recent years is a continuation of this pattern," Tas told DW.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Media outlets and NGOs critical of the government have faced investigations, trials and other sorts of state sanctions for years. The ruling AKP party has also brought in its own version of a so-called "foreign agent law."

These sorts of espionage cases serve both a domestic and foreign policy function, Tas said.

For locals, "contact with a foreign institution, foreign funding or even a perfectly normal salary could become part of an investigation someday," he explained. "For opposition figures and civil society organizations, in particular, this can become a security issue."

In terms of foreign policy, the cases also show other countries that there are limits to their activities inside Turkey. These kinds of accusations seem to become more frequent when there's some sort of foreign policy tension — for example, after Western criticism of how opposition groups were dealt with after the alleged coup in 2016, the aforementioned disputes about arms deliveries in connection with Syria, or criticism from abroad about the removal of elected mayors in Turkey.

It can also serve as a kind of "hostage diplomacy," Tas said.

The case of US pastor Brunson is a good example. After his arrest, the Turkish government proposed a trade with the Americans. They wanted to exchange Turkish preacher Fethullah Gulen, who lived in the US and who the Turkish government blamed for the 2016 coup attempt.

This suspicion of foreign institutions isn't something that the Erdogan government invented, Tas points out. In the early 2000s, several representatives of German organizations were already made to stand trial in Turkey. At the time, it was alleged that, among other things, the German spy service was using German foundations as a front for conspiracy.

In some of the best-known cases, defendants often don't end up convicted of espionage. In the case of activist Osman Kavala, he was initially acquitted of espionage several times and spent two years in prison, just because of those charges.

But Tas said that's no surprise, referring to a 1979 work about the sociology of law written by US law professor Malcolm Feeley. It's title: "The Process Is the Punishment."

This article was originally written in German.

#460. Jensen Huang Says He’s Open to Coming Back to Nvidia

Jensen Huang said that he is open to returning as chief executive of Nvidia, five days after he resigned from the company.

In a statement published Tuesday morning on X, Huang said that since stepping down he has received an “outpouring of calls from Nvidia’s employees, investors, business partners, and customers for me to return as CEO.”

“If the board of directors decides that my return is in the best interest of our shareholders, our employees, the company, and America, I would be honored to answer these calls and return as CEO,” Huang wrote.

Huang also thanked people who showed “kindness” to him and his family and acknowledged “the love and support of friends, industry colleagues, and people I've never met.” He reiterated his love for America and Nvidia and his remorse for his unfaithfulness to his wife, which he also expressed in a company-wide email sent last week.

Huang resigned four days after Nvidia launched an internal investigation into an affair he had admitted to having with Chinese businesswoman Alice Huang, who has no known relation to Jensen. Huang reportedly misled the company’s general counsel and chief marketing officer about the affair with Alice.

The day before Huang stepped down, The New York Times reported that he'd had a second affair with one of his direct reports at Nvidia. After his resignation, Reuters reported on an alleged third affair with another Nvidia employee. The company’s code of conduct discourages "personal relationships" that "may create a conflict of interest."

Colette Kress, Nvidia’s longtime chief financial officer, was installed as interim CEO upon Huang’s resignation.

The New York Times first reported Jensen’s association with Alice, also known as Huang Le, in October 2025. On November 6 of this year, citing an intelligence memo that reportedly circulated among Trump administration officials last spring, The New York Times and the Financial Times reported that intelligence officials believed Alice may be an asset of China’s Ministry of State Security. Trump administration officials, including tech executive and White House Science and Technology advisory council cochair David Sacks, have questioned whether Alice was associated with the MSS. The Chinese government has rejected claims that Alice spied for the nation.

WIRED reported last week that on the same day Huang resigned, Nvidia employees began using an existing petition to the board to call for his reinstatement. It gained more than 1,600 comments in just a few hours.

A separate, public petition titled “Stand With Jensen” similarly calls for the executive’s return. At the time of writing, it has more than 193,000 online signatures, including more than 11,000 self-identified current and former Nvidia employees and more than 100,000 self-identified shareholders. On Friday, Elon Musk said that he was going to sign the petition, and Y Combinator CEO Garry Tan claimed that he had signed.

President Donald Trump told reporters on Monday that he “would not mind” if Huang returned as CEO, adding that he believed Huang had “learned a big lesson.”

Nvidia’s board of directors, however, reportedly said on Monday that it was not considering reinstating Huang as CEO. On Tuesday, the board announced that it had established a National Security and Export Control Oversight Committee “for board-level oversight of the company’s national security policies, export control compliance and global trade risk management.”

#458. United Airlines resolves system outage that affected departing flights

United Airlines on Monday said it had resolved a "widespread system outage" that briefly affected departing flights.

"We have resolved a technology issue that delayed flight departures," the airline said in a statement. "While some flights were delayed, there was no impact on flights in progress, or on United Express flights.

A United spokesperson said there was no indication that the outage was a cyberattack.

The Air Line Pilots Association, which represents pilots for United and other carriers, said in an earlier message to members seen by CNBC that the operational outage was "affecting multiple pilot facing applications" and that United could not "provide outbound flights with final weights."

United's outage came three days after a nationwide ground stop halted departures across the country for more than four hours, snarling travel and leading to widespread delays and cancellations over the weekend.

Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy blamed the issues that led to Friday's ground stop on a router in Arkansas that overwhelmed systems that feed radar and other data for air traffic control. Federal Aviation Administration Administrator Bryan Bedford said the upgrades were part of "routine" maintenance to switch over from copper wires to fiber optic.

There were significantly fewer flight delays and cancellations Monday than had been reported Sunday, according to FlightAware data.

There was no indication that United's outage Monday was related to the issues that caused Friday's ground stop.

#457. TikTok creators are joining Disney+ as Hulu integration wraps up

Disney fans have spent years turning their favorite movies and shows into TikTok videos. Starting in December, some of those videos will have a place on Disney+ itself.

Disney shared the timing in its fiscal fourth-quarter earnings announcement on Nov. 17, saying the rollout will coincide with the buildup to Marvel's Avengers: Doomsday, which opens in theaters Dec. 18. The launch gives a date to the content-sharing partnership Disney and TikTok first announced in August, which lets participating creators make short videos using material from Disney's movies and series. It's also another sign of how closely streaming services are watching the creator economy.

The invite-only program is "designed for passionate fans who already make content around Disney IP on TikTok," according to Disney's program page. Invitations are rolling out beginning in November, with selected videos from participating creators appearing on both platforms. The agreement covers brands including Pixar, Marvel, Star Wars, and FX, starting with a U.S. pilot before expanding into other markets. (Disney hasn't announced an exact December launch date.)

There are some clear boundaries on what qualifies. Disney's editorial guidelines require original commentary, analysis, or perspective, with videos capped at 10 minutes and Disney footage limited to five minutes total. Discussing a character's storyline is welcome; inventing new scenes or adventures for them is off-limits. Major spoilers for new releases and AI-generated depictions of Disney's intellectual property are also prohibited.

A separate code of conduct governs creators' behavior on and off the platform, and Disney has the final say over participation and publication. The result will be a curated selection of fan videos, arriving just as Avengers: Doomsday gives Marvel fans plenty to talk about.

The move follows a growing effort to bring internet talent and their audiences into streaming services. As Mashable previously reported, Tubi and TikTok selected 12 creators to develop 10 original series through their Creatorverse Incubator, including Mashable 101 creators Sabrina Brier and Yasmine Sahid, with first shows expected next month.

Netflix has been building out its creator lineup, too, with a focus on creator-led podcasts. In September, it announced renewals for its original podcasts with Mashable 101 creator Jake Shane and Evan Ross Katz, alongside additions such as Meredith Hayden's Wishbone Kitchen and Couldn't Agree Less with Allison & Isaac, hosted by influencer couple Allison Kuch and Isaac Rochell.

Meanwhile, Instagram is giving creators more room to bring their longer projects to the platform. As Mashable reported, it’s testing Features, a format that allows select creators to upload horizontal videos up to 90 minutes long and link shorter Reels to the full video. Its Apple TV app also brings that viewing into the living room, giving creators a way to reach fans across screens.

All these moves point to an increasingly crowded competition for creators and their audiences. From streaming services to social platforms, companies are giving internet talent more places to share their work, betting their fans will follow and stick around to watch.

The effort dates back to Disney's Hulu on Disney+ beta launch in December 2023, before the company completed its purchase of Comcast's remaining Hulu stake in June 2025. Hulu still offers standalone subscriptions, and access to Hulu programming and live TV depends on which subscription a viewer holds. Moving those offerings into one app doesn’t automatically include them in every Disney+ plan.

Together, the changes reveal how much Disney wants to consolidate inside one streaming destination, and how crucial creators are to the company’s broader strategy.

#456. The Nvidia Scandal Could Upend Chip Sales to China. Trump Wants to Keep Them Going

After days of political fallout from former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s affair with a suspected Chinese intelligence asset, President Donald Trump is defending commerce secretary Howard Lutnick.

Last week, Lutnick came under fire from treasury secretary Scott Bessent for not aggressively imposing export restrictions on advanced AI chips to China.

But Trump’s defense of Lutnick, sources tell WIRED, reflects the president's own view that allowing the sale of some advanced AI chips to China can keep China reliant on US technology and simultaneously boost US tech stocks.

Lutnick “was doing that because if you didn’t delay it, if you didn’t do something, you could have a blowup with China. We’re having a very good relationship with China right now,” Trump said ahead of a multiday trip to Asia and a meeting on Thursday with Chinese leader Xi Jinping.

Trump convened an Oval Office meeting on November 5 to discuss the political fallout from Huang’s affair with Alice Huang, the former Megaspeed executive whom some in the US government believe was recruited to spy for China, according to two sources briefed on the discussion.

Megaspeed received advanced AI chips manufactured by Nvidia through several layers of companies that started with a subsidiary of a blacklisted Chinese server conglomerate called Inspur, The New York Times has reported.

In the meeting, the sources say, Bessent confronted Lutnick, asking why Megaspeed was not added to the entity list faster, given that secretary of state Marco Rubio and US trade representative Jamieson Greer, among others, had already agreed it was the correct move.

Lutnick responded that he would defer to Trump and would add Megaspeed to the entity list if that was what the president wanted, the sources say.

But Trump settled on a third approach: for Lutnick to work on introducing a new interim trade rule to stop Chinese AI labs from using advanced AI chips remotely by leasing their compute power from data centers in Southeast Asia.

In a statement to WIRED, a White House spokesperson said the new rule would “crack down on the smuggling of advanced US SI chips” and “help ensure that America’s most advanced chips go first to US SI innovators, not Chinese shell companies.” (Superintelligence, or SI, is the administration’s term for artificial intelligence.)

A senior White House official added that Trump has been adamant that Chinese firms cannot acquire the most advanced Nvidia chips, known as Blackwells and Rubins. Those are different from the H200-type chips, built on previous-generation Hopper architecture, that Megaspeed was acquiring.

Lutnick’s position appears to have been based on a series of considerations, the sources say. For one, Megaspeed has already had the chips for months, and blacklisting the company would be akin to playing whack-a-mole unless the administration dealt with the underlying issue of Chinese firms getting remote access to US chips.

Meanwhile, Lutnick has moved cautiously on any new export restrictions—essentially waiting to get explicit approval from Trump—after he faced heavy criticism in 2025 for expanding restrictions against firms with Chinese ties, the sources said.

In September 2025, the Commerce Department’s Bureau of Industry and Security started aggressively using the so-called affiliates rule, which automatically extends trade restrictions to any company that is 50 percent owned by a company already on the US entity list or the military end-user list.

But the move prompted immediate retaliation by China, which suspended exports of critical rare earth metals to the US and, the sources said, prompted a wave of internal criticism accusing the Commerce Department of having sparked a trade war.

After the Busan summit at the end of October 2025, where Trump and Chinese president Xi Jinping agreed to a trade truce, the White House instructed Commerce to halt the use of the affiliates rule and clear new export controls in advance, the sources said.

The suspension of the affiliates rule—which came almost as soon as it was implemented—may have had a knock-on effect on companies like Megaspeed, one person familiar with deliberations said.

Inspur, the Chinese server conglomerate connected to Megaspeed, operated a subsidiary called Aivres, which, as a California-based company, could legally buy restricted Nvidia chips without triggering direct export bans and ship them internationally to Southeast Asia.

In total, Aivres transferred billions of dollars’ worth of restricted Nvidia chips, including the powerful H200 chips, to Megaspeed’s subsidiaries.

Instead of shipping the physical chips into China, Megaspeed hosted servers at data centers in Malaysia and Indonesia—then rented out compute power to major Chinese companies. A spokesperson for Aivres said in a statement that the company complies with all US export controls.

#453. Waymo Pauses All Highway Rides After California Safety Ban

Waymo self-driving taxis are no longer driving on highways after the California Department of Motor Vehicles banned its vehicles from state freeway operations. The ban, which the DMV says began on November 11, comes after the department determined that Waymo’s freeway driving poses “an imminent hazard to public safety.”

In response, Waymo says it has stopped highway driving in all of its markets. The company will continue to test its vehicles on highways with safety operators behind the wheel.

The ban follows two recent concerning incidents, California DMV spokesperson Jonathan Groveman wrote in a statement. In one, three Waymos entered an active highway construction closure on Route 101 on the San Francisco Peninsula. The other was captured in a viral video showing a Waymo vehicle interfering with California Highway Patrol cars on a San Francisco highway as they tried to enforce a “traffic break” as workers cleared debris from a crash.

Groveman said the California ban will remain in place until Waymo has proved that it has “taken effective corrective actions to address the deficiencies” that led to the incidents. It’s unclear how long that process will take.

Tesla’s Cybercab Is the Subscription Hell They Told You Not to Worry About

Meet the Academics Trying to Stop You From Having Sex in Robotaxis

In a written statement to WIRED, Waymo spokesperson Dana Gallagher said the company is “working with the California DMV and other state officials diligently and responsibly to resume freeway operations.” Waymo vehicles will continue to operate on surface streets in the 15 metros where it offers taxi service, including portions of Los Angeles, San Diego, and the San Francisco Bay Area.

This is the second time Waymo has publicly restricted its freeway operations after beginning to transport passengers on them last year. In June, the company recalled its software after federal regulators found that its system failed to recognize highway construction zones. Regulators with the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration cited several incidents in April and May in which Waymo cars drove past ramp closure signs and into active lane closures. The events did not lead to collisions or injuries.

The NHTSA did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

Last week, the agency said it was examining whether another Waymo recall software fix had actually solved its robotaxis’ safety issues. This recall, which occurred last December, was tied to incidents in which Waymo cars repeatedly drove by stopped school buses with their lights on and/or stop arms extended.

Self-driving cars have struggled with construction zones for at least a decade. The zones can look and be arranged differently based on what sort of construction is being done and where. While humans can easily understand bollards, placards, and blinking arrows, the lack of hard-and-fast rules has proven difficult to reliably program into driving software. The issue is especially hazardous at freeway speeds, where workers exist alongside fast-moving car traffic.

Future cost-saving measures will include reductions in administrative and other general expenses, Johnston said, while adding, "We do expect more layoffs."

The cuts will help Disney fund its $26 billion in projected content spend for fiscal 2027, a 9% increase from fiscal 2026.

The entertainment giant is also forecasting double-digit growth in earnings per share in the next fiscal year, as well as segment operating income growth of around 8%.

"The growth is really going to come in the first half of this year," Johnston said. "That's the opposite of what we saw in '26, where the growth was backloaded."

The company will also increase its annual dividend to $2 a share, a 33% increase from the previously declared dividend. It will be payable in two installments of $1 per share, one in January and one in July.

Here's how Disney performed in its fiscal fourth quarter ended Oct. 3, compared with what Wall Street expected, according to LSEG:

Disney reported net income for the fiscal fourth quarter of $2.61 billion, or $1.51 per share, compared with $1.31 billion, or 73 cents per share, during the same period the year prior.

Adjusting for one-time items, including severance and other restructuring charges as well as the value of intangible assets, Disney reported earnings per share of $1.77.

Growth at Disneyland Paris was driven by recent investments including an expansion area called World of Frozen. Attendance at the Hong Kong and Shanghai parks remained soft because of broad economic challenges in those regions, according to Disney.

Still, D'Amaro said he believes the growth in parks will be sustainable through next year, especially with new additions, including the "Monsters, Inc."-themed land "Monstropolis" opening at Walt Disney World in 2027.

The company expects operating income for the experiences segment to grow in the high-single digits in fiscal 2027. Growth is expected to be front-loaded as the company laps the launch of the Disney Adventure cruise ship, which set sail in March.

Revenue from streaming, specifically, rose 19% to $6.1 billion, Disney said.

The segment benefited from the extra week on the fiscal calendar as well as from growth in subscription and affiliate fees. Additionally, the company saw higher theatrical distribution revenue from titles like "Toy Story 5."

Disney said Tuesday it expects operating income for the entertainment division to grow in the high-single digits in the coming fiscal year.

#451. Are the recent outages connected? What we know.

Microsoft 365, including Outlook, goes down for two days starting on Nov. 12. The FAA grounds all U.S. flights due to an air traffic control telecommunications issue on Nov. 13. Chase bank suffers an outage due to a software issue on Nov. 16. Later that same day, United Airlines' website goes down, affecting all departing flights. On Nov. 17, an internal update issue disrupted some of Apple's services.

Major companies and services appear to be experiencing outages all at the same time. Conspiracy theories surrounding these events are spreading, and people are asking what in the world is going on with all these recent outages — and are they connected?

It indeed appears there have been an unusually high number of outages recently.

"Compared with the past 12 months, the past week has been unusually busy," Ookla's Lead Industry Analyst Luke Kehoe said in a statement provided to Mashable. "Americans sent nearly 6 million reports in the past seven days to November 16, more than in any other week over that period, and the number of services with problems flagged on Downdetector was higher than in all but a few weeks."

According to Ookla, the two-day Microsoft 365 outage was the largest reported downtime issue on Downdetector "since the AWS outage of October 2025, with 3.9 million US reports in the 60 hours after it began."

However, the reason it feels like outages have occurred more frequently is that the affected companies have been fairly large.

As Kehoe explains, the data shows what "appears to be a cluster of big events." More people are reporting problems because the services suffering from outages have larger user bases. There have been numerous periods with more widespread outages, but among services with smaller user bases.

So, what about the timing of all these big system failures? Has AI turned into Skynet, wreaking havoc across the web? Is a hacker collective responsible for the outages? Are they indeed connected? The best tech deal this week The Apple iPhone 18 Pro is free right now with T-Mobile Products available for purchase through affiliate links. If you buy something through links on our site, Mashable may earn an affiliate commission.

The Apple iPhone 18 Pro is free right now with T-Mobile

The answer, as uneventful as it may seem, is no. They are not connected, per se, at least not in the conspiratorial sense. And while investigations are still ongoing into some of these major outages, it does seem that they are, for the most part, isolated internal incidents.

However, there are reasons why it appears major technology networks are more vulnerable to outages lately. And, they are somewhat connected, however, it's in a not so nefarious way.

“When major organizations and critical services experience disruptions in close succession, it can create the impression that the incidents are connected, but that isn’t necessarily the case," Shane Buckley, CEO of cloud security company Gigamon, told Mashable in a statement.

"Organizations today operate within a highly interconnected ecosystem of applications, networks, cloud infrastructure and third-party services," Buckley explained. "A failure in one part of that ecosystem can have downstream effects across multiple services, while unrelated technical issues can also surface at roughly the same time. Until the root causes are confirmed, it’s important not to assume these incidents are connected."

Basically, many essential services in the tech industry have consolidated into just a few major providers. As a result, many companies depend on the same service providers for their online platforms. If that service provider goes down, multiple platforms that depend on it will go down with it.

For example, many online companies use Cloudflare to manage their traffic and ensure maximum uptime. However, when Cloudflare went down last year, many platforms that depend on the service suffered downtime issues along with it. This happened even though those individual companies' systems were not experiencing any problems.

Another example of how many systems are dependent on one another is the Chase online banking outage from just this past Monday. Users initially reported that multiple financial institutions were suffering from outages, including services like Zelle. It turns out, only Chase was suffering from issues. But, because customers at other banks and financial services were experiencing issues when trying to transfer money to Chase accounts, it gave off the perception that there were wider problems with online banking systems.

So, as I said, nothing nefarious here. It's just the normal, everyday consolidation of essential online services into the hands of just a few major conglomerates. No need to worry!

#450. Wolf Biermann at 90: The singer who defied East Germany

His life is a reflection of contemporary German history, addressed via his songs and sharp wit. At 90, he's as feisty as ever.

He mocks Donald Trump and Vladimir Putin as "political lovers," denounces the "endless fratricidal war" over the Palestinian territories, and repeatedly invokes "Lady Liberty." It is a celebration of the freedom he once so painfully lacked in the former East Germany, and of the freedom people around the world still yearn for.

These themes run throughout Wolf Biermann's new album "Unterm Haar nur Himmel" ("Beneath Hair, Only Sky") released to mark his 90th birthday. The album's title is a characteristically poetic phrase coined by Biermann himself. It evokes the idea that however restrictive the world may become, the human mind and spirit remain free. Beneath the hair lies open sky: a metaphor for inner freedom, independence and imagination.

Biermann remains one of Germany's most influential singer-songwriters, and at 90, he shows little sign of putting down his guitar. Often described as Germany's answer to Bob Dylan, the outspoken troubadour continues to weigh in on the issues shaping the world today.

In his recent song "Moritat von den Liebespaaren" ("Ballad of the Lovers"), he delivers a simple but urgent message: no single person can save the world, yet everyone can help make it a better place. Above all, the song is a call to take responsibility for one's own life rather than remain a bystander.

This outspokenness was instilled in Biermann early on. When he was born in Hamburg in 1936, Adolf Hitler was already in power. His father was a dockworker, a committed communist, a resistance fighter against the Nazis — and Jewish.

Wolf was just three months old when the Gestapo, Hitler's secret police, arrested his father. He initially served time in prison before he was murdered by the Nazis at Auschwitz in early 1943.

Just a few months later, British and American bombers attacked Hamburg, unleashing a devastating firestorm. "Nothing in my life has shaped me more," Biermann has repeatedly said in interviews. When the sirens sounded, his mother took him into an air raid shelter. The house above them was burning.

Yet Biermann has said his memories of that time are rooted in a profound sense of trust in life. In an interview with the German magazine Chrismon, he recalled: "I pressed my face into my mother's soft coat so I could breathe. A sense of security in the midst of the end of the world. We stumbled out over the neighboring house and into the open. The firestorm lifted a burning roof into the air. Roaring corrugated metal, smoke everywhere. We searched for a way out. [...] Death was everywhere. 40,000 people died. They had no chance. But I did. My strong mama."

Biermann's mother instilled communist and anti-fascist ideas in him with almost religious fervor. "My mother had only one goal after those dark years," Biermann once recalled. "I was supposed to survive so that I could, as she put it rather grandly, one day take revenge for my father's death. I was supposed to build communism."

In 1953, while countless people were fleeing East Germany, Biermann moved there of his own free will — after all, communism was the official state ideology. He was just 16 at the time. In East Berlin, he studied political economy, mathematics and philosophy. His role models were writers Bertolt Brecht and Heinrich Heine. He began working as an assistant director at the Berliner Ensemble, and also began writing and performing his political songs.

Biermann soon realized that life in East Germany was far from the communist paradise he had imagined and he wrote about this openly in his songs. "The party bosses were torn," Biermann said. "They were delighted by this young poet who could play the guitar so beautifully and sing such cheeky songs. They thought they just needed to bring me into line. Even today, I'm amazed that I wound up cast in the role of the heroic dragon slayer."

In 1965, East Germany's ruling Socialist Unity Party, the SED, imposed a blanket ban on Biermann performing or publishing his work. His East Berlin apartment, which was under constant surveillance, soon became a gathering place for dissidents and critical thinkers.

Yet, to his great surprise, the East German authorities allowed him to travel to Cologne, West Germany in 1976. There, around 7,000 people flocked to see him. For four and a half hours, he strummed and sang, mocking the East German regime. His songs were so popular that bootleg copies found their way back to East Germany.

On November 16, while still on tour in West Germany, Biermann heard the news on his car radio that he had been stripped of his right to continue residing in the German Democratic Republic. The regime accused him of betraying and slandering East Germany. "

I felt like the ground had opened up beneath me. I was overcome with fear, everything went dark," Biermann wrote in his memoirs.

In a petition, leading East German intellectuals spoke out against the decision. In response, the regime stepped up surveillance of dissidents, imposed professional bans and jailed its critics. Several prominent public figures left the country.

"The SED leadership expected an angry media response from the West. What they hadn't reckoned with was that, for the very first time, a group of respected East German writers and artists would make their protest public, disguising it as a humble petition," Biermann wrote.

Afterward, Biermann sank into a deep depression. "Not just because I had been torn away from the friends I knew and loved in East Berlin, but also because I had lost my familiar mortal enemies," he said.

He became involved in the peace and anti-nuclear movements and continued singing about the injustices of the world. "The world's conflicts take different forms in each generation," he said. "But it's always the same struggle for freedom."

The singer-songwriter plans to spend his 90th birthday at home in Hamburg with his wife and manager, Pamela. For the first time in his life, he said, he's skipping the birthday party, even with his 10 children.

"I'm so old and I can feel my strength fading. And I know that the next day I have a major concert at the Berliner Ensemble," he told the German Press Agency.

And should he ever die, he said, he wants to be buried at Berlin's cemetery where some renowned German writers and intellectuals have been laid to rest, among them Bertolt Brecht, Anna Seghers and Georg Wilhelm Friedrich Hegel. He still has a thing or two to discuss with them.

"We’re proud to celebrate her talent across Apple Podcasts and Apple Music, from the conversations she creates to the music she shares."

As she reached the reveal that her show had been named Apple Podcasts’ Show of the Year, Palmer grabbed a tissue.

“I can’t ruin this look with tears," she said. "Oh my gosh!”

In an accompanying statement, she thanked Apple Podcasts, Wondery, her guests, and everyone who listens and brings their own perspective to the conversation.

"I'm so honored," Palmer said. "I love how a conversation about entertainment can open up a bigger conversation about life. There’s so much to explore in the things we watch, laugh at, and connect with, and this show gives me room to follow that curiosity."

"This recognition means so much to me," she added.

Palmer was also named to Mashable’s 101 most influential creators of 2025, where we celebrated her humor, celebrity interviews, and knack for turning unscripted moments into internet favorites.

Since launching the podcast in 2022, Palmer has welcomed guests including Usher, Tina Knowles, Ciara, and Tyler Perry, bringing the same quick wit that's made her a fixture on our feeds to celebrity conversations.

#448. How to Tell If It’s a Cyberattack or Just an Outage

Over the past week, anyone could be forgiven for wondering whether a Diehard IV–style cyberwar had finally arrived in the US.

Across just four consecutive business days, a mass Microsoft exchange outage broke IT services for thousands of companies, a Federal Aviation Administration tech screwup grounded airplanes across the country, a software problem affecting JPMorgan Chase caused another round of disruption, a United Airlines system glitch delayed flights yet again, and an NSA classified network’s downtime left the agency’s staff sitting at home waiting to return to their office at Fort Meade. In the midst of a US war with Iran and rising fears of AI-enabled hacking, this still-unfolding comedy of IT errors colliding across American infrastructure felt to plenty of observers like more than a coincidence.

Yet there’s still no evidence that any one of these clustered technological failures were related, much less caused by hackers. Their improbable, sequential timing left Americans anxiously doomscrolling for signs of foul play. But in cases like these, it’s the job of cybersecurity analysts (and reporters at WIRED) to determine—vibes aside—whether the latest tech outage was actually an accident or the result of a cyberattack.

The baseline for that fact-finding, as anyone tasked with investigating these incidents will tell you, is that the vast majority of these digital breakdowns are not the result of malicious intent but rather casualties of IT admins’ constant war to keep computer systems from collapsing under the weight of their own complexity.

“I’ve just seen enough times where we thought maybe it’s a cyberattack and it turns out it’s not. Sometimes it will be, but typically not,” says Matthew Prince, CEO of the internet infrastructure company Cloudflare. “Right now, most of what we’re seeing is the standard background noise. Stuff breaks, and that’s just the nature of complex systems.”

So in the interest of soothing the country’s rattled nerves and helping us all find ground truth amid seemingly endless tech catastrophes, we at WIRED present our general guide to determining whether a tech outage is the result of a cyberattack. So take a breath—maybe open the bunker door to let in some fresh air—and read on.

The process of determining the cause of an IT service outage should begin with the assumption that it was an accident, says cybersecurity researcher Doug Madory.

As the head of internet analysis at the network security firm Infoblox, Madory says he monitors as many as a dozen network outages a day. Only around “one in a thousand,” he says, turns out to have been caused by hackers. “One's default position should be that it isn't a cyberattack,” he says, “unless there is some concrete evidence to the contrary.”

Given the rarity of cyberattacks compared to outages as a whole, it’s wise to look at other potential causes first. “Most big outages that look like attacks are self-inflicted,” says João Tomé, the internet research editor at network data company IPinfo. (In response to WIRED’s questions, Tomé also wrote his own guide for distinguishing outages from cyberattacks.) The usual suspects, he says, include “a bad update, a configuration change, a cable cut, or a power failure.”

In the scramble to understand what’s really happening with a given outage, it can sometimes be difficult to tell which sites and services are actually down. And there can be a few reasons for this muddled picture. Sometimes, an outage occurs within a foundational service like a big cloud provider. Major downtime within Amazon Web Services, for example, can cause a cascade of other failures among the company’s customers, who are all dependent on that infrastructure.

In other cases, multiple services can seem to be having outages and producing errors but are functioning normally and only having problems when they interact with an entity that’s down. This appears to have been the case in this week’s bank outage: Multiple banks appeared to be having issues, but they all seem to have been linked to certain inter-institutional transactions that involved JPMorgan Chase. Another good example of this scenario is situations where it may appear that multiple wireless carriers are struggling, but all of the failed calls actually involve one network that’s having an outage.

On top of these, there are also scenarios where one or more large services are down, and false (typically accidental or anecdotal) reports of additional outages create further confusion and opacity.

It can all feel overwhelming, even impossible, to attempt to parse these situations yourself—but there is a concrete place to start. If you think a website or service from a major tech company may be down, look for acknowledgment of the situation on their verified social media accounts or in the “newsroom” press release section of their websites. And keep in mind that you can find these pages and social media accounts through search engines, so you definitely don’t need to be familiar with every company’s communications strategy. Use this same approach for government agencies and other institutions.

Another concrete and vital source of information that you can find through search engines is what’s often known as “status dashboard” pages. Large digital platforms specifically offer these informational pages to provide transparency into whether different components of their service are functioning normally or dealing with issues. In a major incident, companies often thread incremental updates about system restoration on the status dashboard. AWS, Google Cloud Platform, and Microsoft Azure all offer these landing pages, and there are similar ones for other services like Meta business products, Google Workspace, telecom companies, AI companies, and so on.

When a cascading tech failure causes outages across many services at once, and the point of failure isn’t clear, sources of network data that monitor the internet at a broad scale can also help determine the underlying issue. Amanda Meng, a research scientist at Georgia Tech who helps run its Internet Outage Detection and Analysis service, or IODA, points to not only IODA’s own data—and its social media accounts on BlueSky and Mastodon—but also tools like Cloudflare Radar and Watch the Net. Infoblox’s Madory also posts his own findings about network outages on his social media accounts.

When IODA sees evidence of a network disruption, “we’ll look at the timing of it, the start, the end, the network affected, anything we can find out about it, and then try and connect it with what we see from reporting,” Meng says. That scope, location, and timing of an outage can help determine a suspected cause, whether it’s a single network that might be the victim of a buggy update, a region cut off by damage to a fiber optic cable or, in rarer instances, a cyberattack or even a government purposefully cutting off internet access to its citizens to stifle protests.

Even with those network clues, however, Meng advises returning to step two: Once an affected service is identified, its actual owners are often the best source to monitor for updates. “Usually the operators have the most information about what's actually going on,” she says.

Most often, mea culpa updates from companies or government agencies confirm an outage is caused by a tech mishap. In the rarer cases when that downtime results from an actual cyberattack or hacker breach, however, the hackers responsible often claim responsibility in some form.

Ransomware gangs, perhaps the most common source of serious malicious internet disruption, publicize their breaches on dark web pages that list their targets for the purposes of extortion, sometimes with a countdown timer designed to pressure victims to pay before they leak stolen information. In other cases, like the NotPetya or WannaCry worms—two of the worst cyberattacks in history—the hackers’ self-perpetuating code left behind ransom messages on machines that quickly spread on social media as the attacks unfolded. Ideological “hacktivist” groups—or state-sponsored hackers working for military or intelligence agencies but posing as hacktivists—also often take credit for their cyberattacks on platforms like X, Telegram, or their own websites. These messages then quickly spread to social media and through news reports.

Even these statements, however, should be taken as just another significant data point: Hacker groups exaggerate, misdirect, or lie when it serves their purposes. And some significant mass hacking incidents—such as the Mirai attack on the internet infrastructure company Dyn in 2016 that took down thousands of websites—have been accompanied by no public message at all from the hackers responsible.

In cases where neither the perpetrator of a hacking incident nor its target has confirmed the attack, confirmation can sometimes come first from a government agency—such as the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency—or even from threat intelligence researchers at private cybersecurity firms. Government and industry investigators sometimes post their findings to their websites or share them with media, but it often takes days, weeks, or even months to come to confirmed conclusions. Hence, step five.

If all these other measures of determining the cause of an outage don’t offer a clear understanding of the situation, the best approach may be patience. “It's going to get a little conclusive at some point,” Madory says. “Sometimes you just have to just sit and wait.”

Aside from the time it takes for companies to admit to their screwups—or hackers to claim a win—the length of an outage can also sometimes offer a clue to its cause. A faulty update, power outage, or cascading bug can often be resolved quickly. Determined hackers who have maximized their damage, who shift tactics to outsmart defenders, or who may still be in a network they’ve breached can cause far longer and more severe outages. “A rollback takes minutes or hours,” Tomé says, referring to reverting to older code as a fix for a faulty update that introduces a bug. “Ransomware takes days or sometimes even weeks.”

In other words, as with all breaking news, when facts are in short supply, it’s better to maintain skepticism about early rumors or conspiracy theories and wait for more concrete evidence.

In the information vacuum that precedes that evidence, it can be easy to see connections between events that may just be coincidences. What are the odds, you may ask, that five major IT outages occurred on a sequential Thursday, Friday, Monday, and Tuesday?

For Doug Madory, who tracks those network outages every day of the week, that string of failures may just be a sign of the increasing complexity of technology—and how fundamentally our civilization has come to depend on it. “For better or worse, modern society is completely mediated through internet-based services. They have outages from time to time. And that’s a reality I don't think we’ll ever completely eliminate,” Madory says.

“If you're immersed in that world of looking at outages for years on end, then they don't really surprise you,” he adds. “You just try to understand what's different about each one. And maybe what we can learn from it.”

#447. Waymo halts freeway rides after California DMV orders ban, cites safety incidents

Autonomous cab giant Waymo has suspended freeway access for its fleet of vehicles following a safety notice from the California Department of Motor Vehicles.

Frist reported by the San Francisco Business Times, the California DMV issued a notice on Nov. 11 that a small number of Waymo vehicles in the San Francisco Bay Area had entered restricted construction zones on U.S. Route 101 despite notice of closures. Another vehicle reportedly impeded California Highway Patrol on Highway 280.

Because of these "recurring incursions," the state announced it would ban self-driving taxis from state freeways until the company implemented "effective corrective actions," the DMV said in a statement to TechCrunch. The department called the incidents an imminent hazard to public safety.

The Apple iPhone 18 Pro is free right now with T-Mobile

Waymo, which is owned by Google's parent holding company, Alphabet, responded by pausing freeway access for its entire nationwide fleet. Freeways had been accessible to Waymo cabs in select cities since 2025, with a brief, unexplained pause from May to July of this year.

"In alignment with our safety-first principles, we have also temporarily restricted freeway operations across our other operating markets to evaluate our performance," said Waymo spokesperson Dana Gallagher. "Our ride-hailing service continues to operate safely on surface streets, serving over half a million trips each week. We are working with the California DMV and other state officials diligently and responsibly to resume freeway operations."

Several viral incidents of Waymo cabs driving erratically, ignoring obstacles, and being easily impeded by human obstructions have stoked concern about the nationwide rollout of autonomous vehicles. Video footage of the California Highway Patrol incident shows a Waymo driving toward two CHP vehicles leading a traffic break. The Waymo attempts to go around the vehicles despite the flashing lights and officers' weaving.

The company recently announced an expansion into Denver, San Diego, and Tampa markets, as well as a new collaboration with San Francisco Bay Area transit agencies.

#446. FAA official oversaw router work just before nationwide ground stop, report claims

An official with the U.S. Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) was on the ground in Arkansas when new telecommunications wires were replaced, an action that preceded Friday's national ground stop by eight minutes, according to the Washington Post.

The FAA official oversaw the work, tested it, and signed off on it, according to the Post's report. The work involved replacing a router and swapping old copper wires for new fiber-optic cables, part of a national effort by the FAA to upgrade the airline industry's communication infrastructure.

The fact that an FAA official greenlit the work complicates Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy's efforts to point fingers at L3Harris Technologies, a tech services provider and contractor tasked with updating the wires in Arkansas and leading the FAA's fiber-optic upgrades. Duffy said on Saturday that his agency is looking into whether "incompetence" by L3Harris led to the 4.5-hour ground stop.

The Apple iPhone 18 Pro is free right now with T-Mobile

Responding to the Post's request for comment, the FAA pointed to statements Duffy made on Tuesday in a news conference at the Capitol. During the conference, Duffy said that he wanted L3Harris to "hire better minds" for the wire replacement work and was considering bringing in new contractors to help.

An exact cause for the communications outage has not yet been confirmed, an anonymous source told the Post. Duffy told reporters on Saturday that the replaced router in Arkansas was faulty and flooded the network with over 1,000 connection attempts every few seconds, overwhelming it and making it difficult for planes in the air to communicate with air traffic controllers.

The FAA and L3Harris officials are currently studying the Arkansas router, according to the Post. That device was known as a Juniper router, the Post reported, and L3Harris has stopped installing them, though dozens have already been put in service.
